Introduction to Electronic Design Automation (EDA)
The smartphones we use, autonomous vehicles on the road, and even AI servers all run on highly advanced semiconductor chips. These chips contain billions of transistors and intricate circuits, far too complex and time-consuming to design by hand.
Electronic Design Automation (EDA) refers to the software tools and technologies that make it possible to design and verify such chips. With EDA, engineers can automatically draw circuits, optimize layouts, and analyze power and performance. This enables the creation of smaller, faster, and more efficient semiconductors, which serve as the foundation for innovations in AI, autonomous driving, healthcare, and many other fields.
Recently, artificial intelligence and machine learning have also been applied to EDA, helping analyze massive design data and discover improved methods for chip design that would be difficult for humans to achieve alone.
Figure 1. Modern chip design built upon EDA industry
Figure 2. Word Cloud of Design Automation Conference (DAC)
Our Research
Our lab focuses on Electronic Design Automation (EDA) to improve power, performance, and area (PPA) of semiconductor chips by combining heuristic methods with artificial intelligence. Our research covers the full spectrum of chip design, including physical design, analog circuit optimization, standard cell generation, and design-technology co-optimization (DTCO).
We place particular emphasis on applying machine learning (ML) and reinforcement learning (RL) to prediction, optimization, and generation tasks across physical design and design space optimization (DSO).
Our current research is categorized as below (each item links to the corresponding GitHub repository):
Physical Design
Analog Circuit Optimization
Design-Technology Co-Optimization
Standard Cell Generation
ML-based Prediction & Optimization
RL-based Optimization
Design Space Optimization

Introduction
The CTRL(Control Theory, Robotics, and Learning) is a research group of the Department of Electrical Engineering at Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), Pohang, Republic of Korea. The focus of the laboratory is to develop mathematical control theories and their applications to practical control systems such as robotics, aerospace vehicles, cyber-physical systems, and so on.
Open Positions

We especially welcome students who are good at mathematics (e.g., linear algebra, functional analysis, etc.) or programming skills (e.g., C, C++, MATLAB, Python, etc.). If you are interested in joining the Control Theory, Robotics, and Learning, please email here (ctrlpostech@gmail.com ) with an one-page resume.

overview:
At the Control Theory, Robotics, and Learning, we conduct study in the following areas:
Control Theory
We are interested in developing mathematical control theories to solve various difficult problems of control systems, such as stabilization, optimization, and so on. With such a development, we are expected to achieve good performance for practical systems. The detailed research topics considered in the Control Theory & Robotics Laboratory are as follows (but not limited to):
Networked control systems
1) Stability analysis for time-delay in networked control systems
2) Stabilization for time-delay in networked control systems
Hybrid continuous/discrete-time systems (i.e., sampled-data systems)
1) Performance analysis and optimal controller design for persistent disturbances
2) Performance analysis and optimal controller design for impulsive disturbances
Digital redesign of analogue controllers
1) Frequency-domain based redesign scheme
2) Time-domain based redesign scheme
Control Applications
We also aim at providing practical and effective control solutions to the real systems such as robot manipulators, humanoids, and so on. Through such solutions, we are expected to achieve stability and optimality of the real control systems. The detailed research topics tackled in the Control Theory & Robotics Laboratory are as follows (but not limited to):
Robot manipulators
1) Optimal control for dexterous manipulation (e.g., industrial robots)
2) Robust control for stable human-robot interaction (e.g., haptics)
Quadruped Robots
1) Safety recovery of quadruped robots for various disturbance (e.g., Go.2)
2) Walking control of quadruped robots for various disturbance (e.g., Spot)
Mobile Robots
1) Safe navigation of Mobile robots for dynamic disturbance (e.g., Turtle bot, Jackal UGV)
Humanoids
1) Balance control of humanoids for various postures (e.g., seesaw)
2) Walking control of humanoids for various terrains (e.g., pebbles)
Cyber-physical systems
1) Stable tele-operation systems (e.g., surgical robots)
2) Cyber security for adversarial attacks (e.g., power network systems)

overview:
At the Control Theory, Robotics, and Learning, we conduct study in the following areas:
Control Theory
We are interested in developing mathematical control theories to solve various difficult problems of control systems, such as stabilization, optimization, and so on. With such a development, we are expected to achieve good performance for practical systems. The detailed research topics considered in the Control Theory & Robotics Laboratory are as follows (but not limited to):
Networked control systems
1) Stability analysis for time-delay in networked control systems
2) Stabilization for time-delay in networked control systems
Hybrid continuous/discrete-time systems (i.e., sampled-data systems)
1) Performance analysis and optimal controller design for persistent disturbances
2) Performance analysis and optimal controller design for impulsive disturbances
Digital redesign of analogue controllers
1) Frequency-domain based redesign scheme
2) Time-domain based redesign scheme
Control Applications
We also aim at providing practical and effective control solutions to the real systems such as robot manipulators, humanoids, and so on. Through such solutions, we are expected to achieve stability and optimality of the real control systems. The detailed research topics tackled in the Control Theory & Robotics Laboratory are as follows (but not limited to):
Robot manipulators
1) Optimal control for dexterous manipulation (e.g., industrial robots)
2) Robust control for stable human-robot interaction (e.g., haptics)
Quadruped Robots
1) Safety recovery of quadruped robots for various disturbance (e.g., Go.2)
2) Walking control of quadruped robots for various disturbance (e.g., Spot)
Mobile Robots
1) Safe navigation of Mobile robots for dynamic disturbance (e.g., Turtle bot, Jackal UGV)
Humanoids
1) Balance control of humanoids for various postures (e.g., seesaw)
2) Walking control of humanoids for various terrains (e.g., pebbles)
Cyber-physical systems
1) Stable tele-operation systems (e.g., surgical robots)
2) Cyber security for adversarial attacks (e.g., power network systems)

overview:
I’m a part-time theoretician, and a part-time empiricist. I’m interested in how machine learning works.
goals
My long-term goal is to make AI responsible — accessible, sustainable, and righteous.
Currently, I focus on efficient ai, where I aim to characterize the fundamental trade-offs among: (1) accuracy, (2) training cost, (3) inference cost.
tools
As the key tool, I study the algorithmic biases of ML. From a theoretical standpoint, understanding the bias will reveal why certain trade-offs emerge and help us gauge the fundamental limit of the Pareto optimum. From a practical standpoint, harnessing the bias will provide us a crucial tool to achieve the optimal trade-off.
Here are some examples of the biases that I studied:
initialization (a,b). We theoretically characterize how the training speed trades with generalizability, as we change the initialization scale of neural nets.
attention sinks (c, d). We harness the attention-biasing phenomenon to develop a model pre-processing algorithm to improve its post-compression performance.
data transformations. (e) We discover that invertible transformations of the training data can dramatically affect both the training speed and the generalizability, and harness this phenomenon to accelerate neural field training.

overview:
What we do
We focus on various facets of Efficient AI to make AI equally accessible to everyone. In particular, we are interested in achieving the favorable tradeoffs in terms of:
Model accuracy
Inference cost
Training cost
How we approach
We pursue this goal through identifying, understanding and harnessing the algorithmic biases of machine learning. Modern machine learning algorithms tend to be biased toward finding a very specific solution, instead of simply finding any solution which fits the training dataset well. Luckily, it turns out that we can steer ML algorithms in a way that the learned solution generalize well. However, it often comes at the cost of more expensive training or inference.
Through theories, we seek to characterize such tradeoffs; through algorithms, we seek to achieve Pareto-optimal points on the tradeoff curve.
Research highlights
Here are some examples of our recent projects:
Speed, accuracy, and initialization. We characterize how the initialization scale affects the generalizability and training speed of neural networks (A,B).
Adaptation for compression. We develop techniques to improve the performance of compressed models by tuning the models pre- or post-compression (A, B).
On-device LMs that can hear. By crafting new benchmarks, we reveal that on-device LMs often lack auditory commonsense. Then, we mitigate this through retrieval and generation (A, B, C).
Variable-rate compression of deep nets. We devise algorithms to compress neural networks in a way that reflects the distinct roles of each layers (A, B).
Neural codec for model weights. We develop neural data compression algorithms for neural network weights, with applications in LLMs or neural fields (A, B, C, D)
See our papers for more.

overview:
ML models have grown TOO BIG—let’s fix this.
Big models work surprisingly well.
But are also surprisingly bad: (1) Slow inference, (2) Energy- and CO2-heavy training, (3) Requires too much data, (4) Contains many undiscoverable biases, …
EffL aims to resolve this “big model problem” through:
Network Compression
We make neural networks smaller
(e.g., pruning, quantization, distillation, …)
Data Compression
We make the data smaller
(e.g., Image/Video Compression, Dataset distillation, …)
Training Acceleration
We make the model training faster
(e.g., better optimizers/preprocessing, model merging, …)
We hope to gain and utilize expertise on theory, algorithm, and system to give full-stack solutions.

Research Goal
Research Goal
Our goal is to contribute to our society by proposing AI-based algorithms for robots that can coexist with humans.
To achieve this goal, we believe the following three sub-goals need to be completed:
1. Robots need to understand humans.
ex) Action recognition, Emotion recognition, Human pose estimation.
2. Robots need to behace like humans.
ex) Task and motion planning, Human-like motion generation, Imitaion Learning.
3. Robots need to interact with humans.
ex) Behavior planning for natural Human-Robot Interaction (HRI), Human-Human Interation to Human-Robot Interaction.
To this end, we research AI-based Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing, and Motion Planning algorithms.
Note that our final objective is to build a system for natural HRI, by making good use of advanced AI-based perceptual abilities to plan appropriate robotic behavior.

overview:
Since the various combinations of strength and ductility can be achieved in steel, they have found extensive applications across diverse environments. A wide range of mechanical properties can be obtained depending on the alloy compositions and heat treatment processes (temperature, time, and cooling conditions…). We design the alloy compositions and optimize the heat treatment schedule to achieve the desirable mechanical properties. We perform detailed microstructure analyses with these works to understand their new mechanical response. This comprehensive approach enables us to tailor steel production precisely for the intended applications.
The enhanced combination of strength and ductility after optimizing the heat treatment schedule in medium Mn steels

areas.name: Fracture Behavior
areas.text:
Fracture in extreme temperature condition
Fracture of steel in cryogenic and high-temperature environments is a critical issue in applications for extreme temperature conditions. We are researching the main reasons of fracture in extreme temperature conditions (cryogenic (~20 K) and high-temperature (> 800 ℃)). We aim to enhance our understanding of steel’s behavior in these demanding environments by investigating fracture mechanisms and characterizing microstructural changes. Furthermore, we try to suggest some methods to prevent the brittle fracture in extreme temperature conditions.
Improved hot ductility of TWIP steel via MnS inoculation
Improved hot ductility of high-Ni steel via recrystallization after diffusionless transformation
Brittle fracture (intergranular and cleavage fracture)
Brittle fractures can be divided into intergranular(IG) and cleavage fractures according to crack propagation paths. IG fractures in steels are generally related to the local segregation of impurities or precipitation of hard phases at the grain or phase boundary. The segregation behavior at the grain boundaries is not simply associated with exposing temperature and time but is complexly correlated with precipitation behaviors in a matrix and at the grain boundaries. We are researching the correlation between precipitation and segregation and trying to suggest mitigation strategies in various steel, such as lightweight steel, maraging steel, and bcc steel. Cleavage fracture is related to the relative strength difference between theoretical cleavage strength and shear strength. Thus, we investigate intrinsic modulus changes depending on alloying elements to clarify cleavage fracture.
The intergranular fracture after aging by intermetallic compounds precipitation in maraging steel
The intergranular fracture by S segregation in the steel

areas.name: Microstructure Characterization
areas.text:
Advanced Microstructure Characterization
The steel’s properties and performance can be interpreted by microstructure characterization through detailed examination and microscale analysis. It encompasses studying various microstructural features, such as grain boundaries, phases, and crystal defects. By utilizing advanced techniques such as in-situ experiments (in-situ tensile, in-situ heating) and atomic level characterization with Cs-corrected TEM, we are researching to find and interpret veiled mechanisms in various steel, such as TRIP steel, lightweight steel, maraging steel, and so on.
The microstructure evolution of TRIP steels with different cooling rate during tensile test
The formation of inverse-spinel MnAl2O4 in lightweight steel
The evolution of ledge-typed twin boundary in bcc steel
Surface characterization
In the automotive industry, reducing the weight of automobiles has been conducted to increase fuel efficiency. Since this endeavor has led to the substitution with high-strength steel, guaranteeing the corrosion resistance of high-strength steel sheets becomes pivotal in extending the quality assurance period. The corrosion resistance can be enhanced by additional coating, such as painting and conversion coating, and the coating quality is determined by surface characteristics. Therefore, we are researching the correlation of surface characteristics (surface microstructure, surface composition) with surface defects or coating quality. Also, through various methods, modifying surface characteristics to prevent the surface defect or to enhance the coating quality are conducted.
Cross-sectional analysis on the phosphate-missing area with using SEM and TEM

overview:
Since the various combinations of strength and ductility can be achieved in steel, they have found extensive applications across diverse environments. A wide range of mechanical properties can be obtained depending on the alloy compositions and heat treatment processes (temperature, time, and cooling conditions…). We design the alloy compositions and optimize the heat treatment schedule to achieve the desirable mechanical properties. We perform detailed microstructure analyses with these works to understand their new mechanical response. This comprehensive approach enables us to tailor steel production precisely for the intended applications.
The enhanced combination of strength and ductility after optimizing the heat treatment schedule in medium Mn steels

areas.name: Fracture Behavior
areas.text:
Fracture in extreme temperature condition
Fracture of steel in cryogenic and high-temperature environments is a critical issue in applications for extreme temperature conditions. We are researching the main reasons of fracture in extreme temperature conditions (cryogenic (~20 K) and high-temperature (> 800 ℃)). We aim to enhance our understanding of steel’s behavior in these demanding environments by investigating fracture mechanisms and characterizing microstructural changes. Furthermore, we try to suggest some methods to prevent the brittle fracture in extreme temperature conditions.
Improved hot ductility of TWIP steel via MnS inoculation
Improved hot ductility of high-Ni steel via recrystallization after diffusionless transformation
Brittle fracture (intergranular and cleavage fracture)
Brittle fractures can be divided into intergranular(IG) and cleavage fractures according to crack propagation paths. IG fractures in steels are generally related to the local segregation of impurities or precipitation of hard phases at the grain or phase boundary. The segregation behavior at the grain boundaries is not simply associated with exposing temperature and time but is complexly correlated with precipitation behaviors in a matrix and at the grain boundaries. We are researching the correlation between precipitation and segregation and trying to suggest mitigation strategies in various steel, such as lightweight steel, maraging steel, and bcc steel. Cleavage fracture is related to the relative strength difference between theoretical cleavage strength and shear strength. Thus, we investigate intrinsic modulus changes depending on alloying elements to clarify cleavage fracture.
The intergranular fracture after aging by intermetallic compounds precipitation in maraging steel
The intergranular fracture by S segregation in the steel

areas.name: Microstructure Characterization
areas.text:
Advanced Microstructure Characterization
The steel’s properties and performance can be interpreted by microstructure characterization through detailed examination and microscale analysis. It encompasses studying various microstructural features, such as grain boundaries, phases, and crystal defects. By utilizing advanced techniques such as in-situ experiments (in-situ tensile, in-situ heating) and atomic level characterization with Cs-corrected TEM, we are researching to find and interpret veiled mechanisms in various steel, such as TRIP steel, lightweight steel, maraging steel, and so on.
The microstructure evolution of TRIP steels with different cooling rate during tensile test
The formation of inverse-spinel MnAl2O4 in lightweight steel
The evolution of ledge-typed twin boundary in bcc steel
Surface characterization
In the automotive industry, reducing the weight of automobiles has been conducted to increase fuel efficiency. Since this endeavor has led to the substitution with high-strength steel, guaranteeing the corrosion resistance of high-strength steel sheets becomes pivotal in extending the quality assurance period. The corrosion resistance can be enhanced by additional coating, such as painting and conversion coating, and the coating quality is determined by surface characteristics. Therefore, we are researching the correlation of surface characteristics (surface microstructure, surface composition) with surface defects or coating quality. Also, through various methods, modifying surface characteristics to prevent the surface defect or to enhance the coating quality are conducted.
Cross-sectional analysis on the phosphate-missing area with using SEM and TEM

In the Clean Steel Laboratory (CSL) of the Graduate Institute of Ferrous and Eco Materials Technology and jointly associated with Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Pohang University of Science and Technology, we are aiming to contribute to our academic community and steel industry by carrying out research, education, and communication. The main research area of interest is chemical metallurgy, including chemical thermodynamics, kinetics, and solidification. The practical application area includes the pyrometallurgical process, in particular for steelmaking and continuous casting processes.
We are looking for students and post-docs who are interested in high-temperature process metallurgy including molten steel cleanliness (chemical refining and inclusion control), ferrous scrap and Li-ion battery recycling, hydrogen production, hydrogen ironmaking, low C emission steel production via chemical metallurgical principles (thermodynamics, kinetics, physicochemical properties of melts, etc.). If you are interested in carrying out the research at CSL, please contact Dr. Youn-Bae Kang.
If you are interested in this position, please contact Dr. Youn-Bae Kang.

Home
Clean Steel Laboratory,
Graduate Institute of Ferrous and
Eco Materials Technology,
Department of Materials Science and Engineering (JA),
Pohang University of Science and Technology
In the Clean Steel Laboratory (CSL) of the Graduate Institute of Ferrous and Eco Materials Technology and jointly associated with Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Pohang University of Science and Technology, we are aiming to contribute to our academic community and steel industry by carrying out research, education, and communication. The main research area of interest is chemical metallurgy, including chemical thermodynamics, kinetics, and solidification. The practical application area includes the pyrometallurgical process, in particular for steelmaking and continuous casting processes.
We are looking for students and post-docs who are interested in high-temperature process metallurgy including molten steel cleanliness (chemical refining and inclusion control), ferrous scrap and Li-ion battery recycling, hydrogen production, hydrogen ironmaking, low C emission steel production via chemical metallurgical principles (thermodynamics, kinetics, physicochemical properties of melts, etc.). If you are interested in carrying out the research at CSL, please contact Dr. Youn-Bae Kang.
If you are interested in this position, please contact Dr. Youn-Bae Kang.

overview:
● 미래 모빌리티용 고기능 철강소재 (Advanced steels for future mobility)
자동차를 비롯한 다양한 모빌리티의 에너지 효율 향상과 승객 안전성 확보를 위하여 초고강도와 고성형성을 겸비한 철강소재에 대한 요구가 점점 높아지고 있습니다. Dual-phase (DP) steels, Transformation-inudced plasticity (TRIP) steels, Twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) steels, Quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels 등 모빌리티용 철강소재의 성능을 극한으로 향상시키기 위한 연구와 더불어 Heterogeneity-driven microstructure control과 같이 고기능 금속재료 설계의 패러다임을 바꿀 수 있는 새로운 개념의 미세조직 제어 원리와 응용 가능성에 대해 연구하고 있습니다
● 미래 인프라용 내수소취성 소재 (Highly reliable steels under non-friendly environment)
철강소재의 초기가 강도화에 따라 기존의 철강소재에서는 문제가 되지 않았던 내환경 안정성에 대한 문제가 대두되고 있습니다. 대표적인 것이 수소에 의한 취성 발생 (hydrogen embrittlement) 입니다. 수소취성은 초고강도 철강소재 내에 존재하는 미량의 수소에 의해서 연성이 급속이 저하되어 예기치 못한 파괴가 발생하는 현상을 의미합니다. 수소에 의한 철강소재의 물성 열화 대해서는 아직 통일된 견해가 존재하지 않으나 여러가지 복합적 원인에 의해 발생하는 것으로 알려지고 있습니다. 수소에 의한 철강소재 물성 열화 극복을 통해 초고강도 강재를 안전하게 활용할 수 있도록 수소취성의 발생기구 및 다양한 초고강도강에서의 물성 열화를 방지할 수 있는 원천기술에 대해 연구하고 있습니다.
우리 연구실에서는 상변태에 기반한 금속소재 설계 및 극한환경 대응 기술 연구를 통하여 미래 모빌리티, 에너지 산업 및 지속가능한 미래사회 인프라 구축을 위한 핵심소재인 차세대 철강재료 및 금속소재에 대해 연구하고 있습니다.
열역학 / 속도론 및 첨단 분석 기법을 활용한 미세조직 형성기구 해석과 합금 / 공정설계에 기반한 혁신 미세조직 제어 기술 연구를 통해 현재 사용되고 있는 철강/금속소재의 한계를 획기적으로 뛰어넘을 수 있는 새로운 재료설계의 패러다임을 제시하기 위한 연구를 수행하고 있습니다.
● 우주 및 항공용 차세대 금속소재 (Innovative alloys for aero-space application)
우주/항공용 금속재료는 경량화와 더불어 다양한 구조 및 열적 특성을 만족하여야 합니다. 대표적인 소재가 위성체에 사용되는 극저열팽창 금속소재 입니다. 위성체에 활용되는 소재는 구조적 신뢰성 뿐만 아니라 치수 안정성 확보를 위하여 온도의 변화에 따른 열팽창 특성을 극소화할 필요가 있는데 경량화, 초고강도 및 고인성, 극저열팽창 특성을 겸비한 금속소재 개발은 미래 우주/항공분야의 독자적인 기술 영역 확보를 위해 핵심적인 분야라 할 수 있습니다. 이를 위하여 우리 연구실에서는 Multiformity Integration-based Novel Design (MIND) 개념에 기반하여 금속소재의 미세조직을 극한으로 제어함으로써 기존 소재의 성능한계를 돌파할 수 있는 미래소재 설계기술에 대해 연구하고 있습니다

overview:
Research Project
Research Project
Total 4건 1 페이지
Battery Microstructure Optimization
We are performing the large-scale simulations to predict cathode (e.g., NCM cathode) microstructure evolution with time and temperature during the sintering process.
The ultimate goal of this project is to investigate the underlying physics behind the sintering phase transformation based on thermodynamics and kinetics for high-performance energy storage battery cathode.
위탁기관) 포스코홀딩스 미래기술연구원 AI연구소
Atomic-Scale Battery Design
We are performing an atomic-scale analysis of the energetics of the cathode (e.g., Li- and Mn-rich layered structure cathode) to understand thermodynamic stability depends on crystal structure and composition.
The ultimate goal of this project is to optimize the high voltage, long lifespan, and superior mechanical stability in designing advanced cathode materials for the next-generation energy source.
위탁기관) 한국산업기술진흥원 (포스코홀딩스, 삼성SDI)
Additive Manufacturing
We are performing an atomic-scale analysis of solute diffusion, the large-scale simulations of microstructure evolution, and machine-learning-assisted model development for mechanical property prediction.
The ultimate goal of this project is to design new Additive Manufacturing (AM) structural materials with high strength and high thermal resistance for the next-generation manufacturing landscape.
위탁기관) 국방부 방위사업청, 한국연구재단
Electrical Steel
We are performing the experimental characterization and the large-scale simulations to understand microstructure evolution in steels (e.g., electrical steel).
The ultimate goal of this project is to investigate the mechanism of phase transformations (e.g., recrystallization, grain growth) and achieve high magnetic properties (minimum iron loss) of electrical steels for high performance of transformers, electric motors, and generators.
위탁기관) 포스코 기술연구원

overview:
Home > Research Area
In CSP laboratory, we conduct the research on various topics. Each topics share the fundamental idea of advanced solidification concepts. Based on this theory, our lab strives to understand and study the solidification behavior of materials widely used in industrial fields such as nuclear power plant and steel making company. Research criteria are followed as 5 parts:
Controlling Solidification Structures of Cast Materials
Cu-Fe alloy is a typical alloy system in which phase separation occurs in the liquid state due to its positive enthalpy and wide solid-liquid coexistence region. When the austenitic phase nucleation occurs earlier than liquid phase separation during the solidification process, the liquid phase separation behavior can be controlled. Based on these facts, the optimal inoculant element for Copper-Ferrous alloy and medium entropy alloy (MEA) composition could be found from using thermodynamical calculations, and the process of phase transformation. Texture and microstructural analysis are considering the specimen produced with vibration technical casting machine (VTC) and analyzed with differential scanning calorimeter (DSC).
<1. Controlling Solidification Structures of Cast Materials>
Thermo-physical properties of oxide glasses and mold fluxes
In order to understand atomic-scale structure in a multi-oxide glass in a detail, it is necessary to control its physical and chemical properties. Especially “Borosilicate glass” has been adopted for various usage, including matrices for immobilization of high-level radioactive nuclear waste, mold fluxes for continuous casting of high Al-steels, and sealing materials for solid oxide fuel cells. By using complementary tools such as solid-state magic-angle spinning (MAS) NMR, vibrational spectroscopy, XAFS, and molecular dynamics (MD) for structural analysis of glass.
Furthermore, controlling the heat transfer and providing lubrication in a casting mold is the most essential in conventional casting process. These following functions will govern by various physical properties of mold flux, such as thermal conductivity and viscosity which is desirable to understand both the structure and properties. Heat transfer phenomena in casting mold strongly depends on the crystallization behaviors of mold flux such as melting crystallization kinetics and morphological evolution of crystalline phase.
Thus, we are aiming on fundamental but extremely relevant studies on thermo-physical properties of multi-oxide glasses and mold fluxes. Development of advanced multi oxide glass systems topics can be conclude as follow:
1) Structural Elucidation of Mixed Ion Effect in Oxide Glasses
2) Effect of Li2O on CaO-SiO2-CaF2-based Mold Flux
3) Heat Transfer control by dispersed metallic particles in glassy mold flux
4) Increase Mo solubility in Mo glass by structural stabilization.
<2. Thermo-physical properties of oxide glasses and mold fluxes>
Additive manufacturing process
Additive Manufacturing (AM) process also known as 3D printing is a construction of 3D model by specifying single layer of material transported from 3d CAD file. The 3D bulk specimen manufactured by AM is being applied in various fields of industry due to its finer microstructure and superior mechanical properties than that of the conventional casting process. The analysis on chemical metallurgy-based metal AM research starts from understanding microstructural changes based on the advanced solidification theory.
For our research scope, we use both powder bed fusion type printer and direct energy deposition type to observe the microstructural tendency, application method and strengthening mechanism by formation behavior of inclusions such as nitride and oxide.
In addition, we are exploring the strengthening effect and thermodynamical analysis of inclusions and precipitates generated during rapid solidification through controlling the cooling rate and shielding gas flow rate.
Furthermore, our group focuses on various experiments such as controlling the difference in solidification behavior between heterojunctions functionally graded material and analyzing microstructural changes by simulation method and thermodynamical calculations.
<3. Additive manufacturing process>
Radioactive waste management
There are various types of radionuclides in nuclear fuel waste that must be disposed safely and isolated from the human society. In order to separate radionuclides from nuclear fuel waste, nuclear waste recycling process like ‘pyro process’ is performed, which leads separation of radionuclides such as radioactive rare earth, Technetium (Tc), Iodine (I), Cesium (Cs) and Strontium (Sr).
Hazardous radionuclides immobilized into a glass form (vitrification process) and disposed underground, efficiency in terms of volume reduction with chemical stability could achieve that is possible to alleviate social and economic burden by reducing the size of the repository site.
In our laboratory, we are conducting research such as the development of a glass solidified material capable of carrying radionuclides for a long-term period, and the investigation of their radiation effects, physical stability, and glass structure by using analysis methods such as XRF, NMR, Raman, and EXAFS.
Computational Material Science
Material’s property could be varied from the compositional and structural changes of material. Conventional experimental method has been reported as erroneous method which is time consuming with repetitive trials to find the ultimate calculation.
Our research group majorly performs Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulation, Machine Learning (ML), Finite Element Method (FEM), Density Functional Theory (DFT) and Monte Carlo Simulation (MC) to figure metal material with glass ceramic materials’ mechanical property and chemically stable structural composition analysis.
<5. Computational Material Science>

overview:
● 미래 모빌리티용 고기능 철강소재 (Advanced steels for future mobility)
자동차를 비롯한 다양한 모빌리티의 에너지 효율 향상과 승객 안전성 확보를 위하여 초고강도와 고성형성을 겸비한 철강소재에 대한 요구가 점점 높아지고 있습니다. Dual-phase (DP) steels, Transformation-inudced plasticity (TRIP) steels, Twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) steels, Quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels 등 모빌리티용 철강소재의 성능을 극한으로 향상시키기 위한 연구와 더불어 Heterogeneity-driven microstructure control과 같이 고기능 금속재료 설계의 패러다임을 바꿀 수 있는 새로운 개념의 미세조직 제어 원리와 응용 가능성에 대해 연구하고 있습니다
● 미래 인프라용 내수소취성 소재 (Highly reliable steels under non-friendly environment)
철강소재의 초기가 강도화에 따라 기존의 철강소재에서는 문제가 되지 않았던 내환경 안정성에 대한 문제가 대두되고 있습니다. 대표적인 것이 수소에 의한 취성 발생 (hydrogen embrittlement) 입니다. 수소취성은 초고강도 철강소재 내에 존재하는 미량의 수소에 의해서 연성이 급속이 저하되어 예기치 못한 파괴가 발생하는 현상을 의미합니다. 수소에 의한 철강소재의 물성 열화 대해서는 아직 통일된 견해가 존재하지 않으나 여러가지 복합적 원인에 의해 발생하는 것으로 알려지고 있습니다. 수소에 의한 철강소재 물성 열화 극복을 통해 초고강도 강재를 안전하게 활용할 수 있도록 수소취성의 발생기구 및 다양한 초고강도강에서의 물성 열화를 방지할 수 있는 원천기술에 대해 연구하고 있습니다.
우리 연구실에서는 상변태에 기반한 금속소재 설계 및 극한환경 대응 기술 연구를 통하여 미래 모빌리티, 에너지 산업 및 지속가능한 미래사회 인프라 구축을 위한 핵심소재인 차세대 철강재료 및 금속소재에 대해 연구하고 있습니다.
열역학 / 속도론 및 첨단 분석 기법을 활용한 미세조직 형성기구 해석과 합금 / 공정설계에 기반한 혁신 미세조직 제어 기술 연구를 통해 현재 사용되고 있는 철강/금속소재의 한계를 획기적으로 뛰어넘을 수 있는 새로운 재료설계의 패러다임을 제시하기 위한 연구를 수행하고 있습니다.
● 우주 및 항공용 차세대 금속소재 (Innovative alloys for aero-space application)
우주/항공용 금속재료는 경량화와 더불어 다양한 구조 및 열적 특성을 만족하여야 합니다. 대표적인 소재가 위성체에 사용되는 극저열팽창 금속소재 입니다. 위성체에 활용되는 소재는 구조적 신뢰성 뿐만 아니라 치수 안정성 확보를 위하여 온도의 변화에 따른 열팽창 특성을 극소화할 필요가 있는데 경량화, 초고강도 및 고인성, 극저열팽창 특성을 겸비한 금속소재 개발은 미래 우주/항공분야의 독자적인 기술 영역 확보를 위해 핵심적인 분야라 할 수 있습니다. 이를 위하여 우리 연구실에서는 Multiformity Integration-based Novel Design (MIND) 개념에 기반하여 금속소재의 미세조직을 극한으로 제어함으로써 기존 소재의 성능한계를 돌파할 수 있는 미래소재 설계기술에 대해 연구하고 있습니다

areas.text:
Home Research Nano Severe Plastic Deformation
Nano Severe Plastic Deformation (NSPD)
Nano Severe Plastic Deformation (NSPD) is a representative method for manufacturing a nanocrystalline metals by applying ultra-high plastic strain.
The improvement of hardness and yield stress can be investigated using SPD process, and the superplastic behavior of these materials behaves at lower temperatures with higher strain rates.

areas.name: Machine Learning
areas.text:
Home Research Machine Learning
Multi-Scale and multiphysics models can be used along very different research and engineering directions. The most prominent field of multiscale materials modeling lies in predicting relations between structure, processing and properties of complex materials beyond the regimes that have been probed experimentally. Another important field of high interest in that context lies in the use of models for predicting so far unknown materials structures, properties or performance. The third essential field lies in developing adequate multiscale models that can be used for process simulation, in the best case even for online structure - property predictions of materials during manufacturing.

areas.name: High Entropy Alloy
areas.text:
Home Research High Entropy Alloy
For the past decade and a half a new alloying strategy that involves the combination of multiple principal elements in high concentrations to create new materials called high-entropy alloys has been emerging. High-entropy alloys have greatly expanded the compositional space for alloy design. The multidimensional compositional space that can be tackled with this approach is practically limitless, and only very small compositional regions have been investigated so far. Nevertheless, a few high-entropy alloys have already been shown to possess good mechanical, magnetic and invar properties, exceeding in part those of some conventional alloys, and more such high-entropy alloys are likely to be discovered in the future.

areas.name: Sheet Formability
areas.text:
Home Research Sheet Formability
Sheet metal forming, the most cost-effective procedure for manufacturing is essential in the industry. Numerous metal products found in our daily lives are made by forming from small parts like soda cans to automobile bodies and construction parts. It is of importance to evaluate the formability of the material to be formed in desire shapes without failure. This formability has been in an important position in the industry, and research has been carried out for a long time. In particular, in the situation where several new materials such as high entropy alloys are emerging today, formability will pave the path for the commercialization of various developing materials.

I am an Associate Professor at CSE, Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), where I am leading Computer Architecture and Operating Systems (CAOS) Laboratory together with Prof. Jisung Park. Before joining POSTECH in March 2025, I worked as an associate professor at DGIST (from July 2017 to February 2025) and an assistant professor at Inha University (from March 2016 to June 2017), respectively. I was a postdoctoral associate in the Computation Structures Group (CSG) at MIT CSAIL advised by Prof. Arvind. At MIT, I worked on the development of system software for big-data analytic systems and non-volatile memory systems. I earned the PhD and MS degrees in computer science and engineering from the Seoul National University (SNU) in 2013 and 2007, respectively, and received the BE degree in electrical engineering from the Korea University in 2005. At SNU, I was a member of the Computer Architecture and Embedded System Laboratory (CARES) led by Prof. Jihong Kim. My current research interests include operating systems, system software, storage/memory systems, and AI systems.

Welcome!
I am an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at POSTECH. I am leading Computer Security Lab.
My research vision is to develop automated systems for analyzing safety-critical computer-based systems. In particular, I am deeply passionate about investigating and improving the security and robustness of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), which encompass practical systems such as drones, self-driving vehicles, robotic systems, and the Internet of Things (IoT) devices.
For prospective students
I am looking for creative and ambitious students who are interested in general cybersecurity, cyber-physical systems, robotics, operating systems, hacking, and ML/AI. Please feel free to reach out to me via email with your CV and transcript.

Research
Problems
Methods
Graph Problems
Planar and Surface Graphs
We stduy combinatorial properties of planar graphs and suface graphs with bounded genus and design algorithms using these properties.
Geoemtric Intersection Graphs
We study combinatorial properties of unit disk graphs, disk graphs, and outerstring graphs, and design algorithms using these properties.
Geometric Problems
Clustering Problmes
We study clusting problems including the k-center problem and k-means problems under various settings.
Range Searching Problems
We develop data structures for geometric problems such as range-clustering problems and shortest path problems.
Efficient Algorithms
Parameterized Algorithms
For NP-hard problems, our goal is to design efficient FPT algorithms.
Here, we measure the running time of an algorithm w.r.t. the input size and a parameter.
Polynomial-Time Algorithms
For problems in class P, our goal is to design linear/quadratic time algorithms.
Computational Complexity
Conditional Lower Bounds
Assuming P≠NP (or ETH), we prove lower bounds on the computation times for various algorithmic problems.
Matching Lower Bounds
Our main purpose of studying lower bounds is to show that our algorithms are optimal.

overview:
Research Topics
Disjoint Paths on Planar Graphs
In this paper, we study the Planar Disjoint Paths problem: Given an undirected planar graph with n vertices and a set of k pairs of vertices, the goal is to find a set k pairwise vertex-disjoint paths connecting each pairs.
We present an FPT-algorithm for the Planar Disjoint Paths problem which takes linear time depends on n and single exponential time depends on k. This improves the two previously best-known algorithms: linear in n time but double exponential in k time algorithm [Discrete Applied Mathematics 1995] and single exponential in k but n to the 6 time algorithm [STOC 2020].
FVS on Unit Disk Graphs
Given an undirected graph, the FVS(Feedback Vertex Set) problem asks for finding a minimum number of vertices whose removal makes the graph acyclic. We study this problem on unit disk graphs (UDGs). Disks in the plane forms a vertices of UDG, and two vertices are connected by an edge of UDG if their corresponding disks are intersect each other.
The FVS problem is NP-hard, but in the parametrized complexity theory, we analyze the running time of an algorithm with respect to the input size and a new parameter. Here, we use the solution size as a parameter.
In this work, we present an ETH-Tight algorithm for the FVS problem on unit disk graphs. In other words, if there is an algorithm faster than our algorithm, it disobeys ETH hypothesis, which is a stronger version of P!=NP hypothesis.
Random Geometric graphs
Geometric random graphs can be models for many real-world graphs. In this work, we focus on hyperbolic random graphs. A hyperbolic random graph can be considered as a mathematical model for analyzing scale-free networks since it effectively explains the power-law degree distribution of scale-free networks.
Using randomness and geometrical properties, various algorithms can be improved using average-case analysis. In this work, we present efficient algorithms for computing a maximum clique problem. We evaluate the performance of our algorithm theoretically and practically.
Distance Oracles for Geometric Graphs
In this work, we study approximate distance oracles for fault-tolerant geometric graphs. Given a geometric graph G, our goal is to design a data structure using linear space so that, given two query vertices and a set of failed vertices, an approximate distance between the two query vertices avoiding the failed vertices can be computed efficiently.
In general, no data structure for this problem using subquadratic space exists. In this work, using geometric tools, we presented a data structure for this problem on geometric graphs using near-linear space.

Soluble Inorganics
Facile dissolution of inorganics can offer a convenient route to exploit inorganic materials as sintering aids of mesoscale particles, ligands for nanoparticles and precursors for wet-chemical deposition of thin films. Inorganic materials can be directly dissolved in nucleophilic environment induced by excess chalcogen in hydrazine or deprotonated thiol in solvent mixture with amine. The nucleophiles in these solvents react with bulk inorganics breaking down them into molecular inorganic anions. Moreover, such inorganic molecules could be synthesized by traditional coordination chemistry route. We study for basic understanding on the role of molecular inorganics interacting with micro- and nano-scale building blocks, and utilize them for 2D or 3D architecturing of functional materials.

Extrusion-based 3D Printing
Extrusion-based additive manufacturing is the most fundamental form of 3D printing, relying entirely on the rheological properties of the printing ink. Therefore, the formulation of inks with tailored rheological behavior and functional performance is essential for fabricating architectured materials that exhibit high electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties. To address this need, our research focuses on the development of organic-free, inorganic particle-based colloidal inks, alongside the optimization of compatible extrusion-based printing processes.
Viscoelastic ink formulation
For the dispensing printing method, the ink must exhibit non-Newtonian and viscoelastic behavior, which facilitates reliable extrusion flow through the nozzle to prevent clogging, and high elasticity to avoid the collapse of the 3D structure. These inks are often paired with polymer-based organic binders to give rise to viscoelastic behavior. However, functional properties of these composite-type inks with polymer additives are strictly limited due to the intrinsically limited electrical properties of organic binders. To overcome this limitation, we have developed molecular chalcogenidometallate-based (ChaM) ions, anions containing metal atoms ligated with chalcogens. We design the rheological properties of TE ink through surface engineering such as ChaM ion addition, doping, etc.
Extrusion-based 3D printing process
Our group developed an extrusion-based 3D printing process for viscoelastic inks that enables the fabrication of functional materials into 3D shapes. In this printing process, ink is dispensed out of the nozzle directly to the substrate by pneumatic control. The printing process enables precise micro-scale 3D printing by reducing the particle size in the ink or the nozzle size while controlling the process parameters. This developed 3D printing process allows for increased freedom in designing materials and devices.

Thermoelectrics
Thermoelectrics is a rapidly evolving field centered on the direct interconversion of heat and electricity through the Seebeck and Peltier effects. This unique capability enables the development of solid-state devices that can generate electricity from waste heat or provide localized cooling without any moving parts, fluids, or greenhouse gas emissions. As global energy demands continue to rise alongside the urgency for sustainable and efficient technologies, thermoelectric materials and devices have attracted significant attention across both academia and industry. Their potential spans a wide range of applications—from powering remote sensors and wearable electronics to recovering waste heat in industrial processes and enhancing the efficiency of automotive and aerospace systems. However, the widespread adoption of thermoelectrics remains limited by the challenge of simultaneously optimizing their electrical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and thermal conductivity. Addressing this challenge requires innovative strategies in materials design, architecture optimization, and system integration. In our research, we explore novel approaches to maximize the thermoelectric energy conversion efficiency through the development of 3D designs and printing of thermoelectric architectures and advanced materials. As well, we develop cost-effective manufacturing methods for efficient thermoelectric devices by 3D printing.

tabs.label: Nanocrystals
tabs.text:
Nanocrystals
Nanocrystals are crystals between 1 and 100 nm in size with a surrounding interfacial layer, attracting huge attention from various disciplines because of their unique properties which are different from conventional bulk materials, high surface to volume ratio and easily controllable properties by size, shape and composition. These nanocrystals as building blocks affords “artificial atoms” to grow or to architecture designed solids with tailored electronic, magnetic, and optical properties. Following colloidal nanocrystal solution can be easily fabricated to solid-state device with various solution process across a wide range of applications like electronic, optoelectronics, catalyst, etc. We have endeavored to synthesize various nanocrystals with different size, shape and composition across various material types such as metals, semiconductors, and oxides by the colloidal chemical route to adopt nanocrystals as effective building blocks and characterize those nanocrystals to observe changes in properties according to conditions. Our goal is to fabricate multi-dimensional architectures through various processes using colloidal nanocrystal building blocks exhibiting unique and tailored properties.

tabs.label: Surface Chemistry
tabs.text:
Surface Chemistry
One of the key parameters to synthesize robust and well crystalline nanocrystals of defined morphologies and function is the choice of surface ligands. Ligands play multiple roles ranging from the regulation of the solubility and availability of active components during NP synthesis to the post synthetic minimization of surface energy of nanocrystals (required for their colloidal stability) as well as the encoding of nanocrystals. We aim to chemically design the surfaces of nanocrystals by developing new-typed inorganic ligands for controlling over their functional properties as well as programming their many-body interactions in a solid. Designed nanomaterials can be applied to electronics, optoelectronics, catalysts, energy materials and 3D printing building block by processing.

tabs.label: Design & Optimization
tabs.text:
Design & Optimization
The design and optimization of 3D architectures are critical for enhancing structure-induced functionalities, thereby improving performance in real-world applications. Such strategies enable engineers to maximize energy efficiency, minimize losses, and tailor thermoelectric systems to accommodate diverse boundary conditions. To this end, we employ finite element modeling (FEM) to design materials and devices with target-specific properties for applications in thermoelectrics and electronics. This effort is complemented by topology and geometric optimization techniques. Furthermore, we are establishing new design principles grounded in fundamental multiphysics, which not only deepen scientific understanding but also enable transformative, real-world solutions for clean and efficient energy technologies.

tabs.label: Solution-processed Thin Films
tabs.text:
Solution-Processed Thin Films
Solution-based processing has attracted huge attention for its advantages of large-scale and cost-effective fabrication of various applications. We are synthesizing novel all-inorganic inks comprising soluble inorganic precursors or nanocrystals for the fabrication of thin films with tailored composition, structure, and properties. The materials of interest include semiconducting metal chalcogenides and phosphorus, metallic Ag, Cu, and 2D MXenes, applied to semiconductor and memory devices.

tabs.label: Nano 3D Architecturing
tabs.text:
Nano 3D Architecturing
Nano 3D printing is a technology included in the world’s 50 innovation technology in Frost & Sullivan 2017 report. Nano 3D printing could play an important role in micro-, and nano- scale 3D fabrication such as MEMS. We are developing novel nanocrystal inks and processing for designing nano-scale 3D architecture with tailored structure and properties. We design stimuli-responsive, assembly-programmable nanocrystal building blocks through chemical engineering of surfaces and interfaces. To this end, we are exploring fundamental chemistry and physics governing the assembly of nanocrystal building blocks under various external stimuli. Architectured 3D matters will find potential applications of 3D electronics, sensors, catalysts as well as a platform of lithography.

tabs.label: Electronics
tabs.text:
Electronics
We are developing novel all-inorganic inks composed of molecular inorganic complexes and nanocrystals, specifically tailored for applications in semiconductor and memory devices. These functional inks enable the fabrication of high-performance devices through solution-processed thin films or precisely patterned arrays achieved via nanoscale 3D architecturing techniques. Our research aims to expand the application scope of these materials, exploring their potential in next-generation semiconductors, non-volatile memory systems, and emerging electronic platforms that demand scalable, cost-effective, and high-resolution manufacturing approaches.

tabs.label: Catalyst
tabs.text:
Catalyst
Catalysts are necessary parts for chemical reactions, which control the overall reaction rates. As the further decrease of the size of materials to nanometer scale, their electrical and physical properties can be changed. One of the fascinating properties of nanomaterials is a high surface-to-volume ratio, which maximizes catalytically active sites. Also, the usage of noble metal (e.g. Pt, Pd) can be drastically reduced as the efficiency of the catalyst is maintained. We are synthesizing platinum and other transition metals based catalytic nanoparticles for high catalytic efficiency and further designing catalyst precursors for improved durability and stability.

Research Area
Research Area
Use soft things to solve hard problems
The overall aim of our research is to understand and control the structure and dynamics of soft matter at interfaces in dimensions ranging from nano- to macroscale and engineer new functional materials. A key aspect of our research is the preparation of well-defined molecules, materials, emulsions and surfaces, which leads to desired function.
Interface engineering
Microfluidics
Encryption and Display
Artificial cell
Healthcare and Sustainability
Wetting
The ability to control surface wettability plays an important role in many applications, from antifogging and self-cleaning surfaces to enhancing condensation. By manipulating surface energy and microstructural design, we aim to develop hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces tailored for specific functionalities. These designs enable the effective management of water droplets, leading to advancements in antifogging coatings, liquid-repellent surfaces, and more.
Hydrogel
Hydrogels, known for their high water content and tunable mechanical properties, serve as versatile materials in designing functional interfaces. We explore their applications in creating antifogging layers, responsive coatings, and soft actuators. By adjusting chemical compositions and crosslinking densities, we tailor hydrogels to exhibit specific responses to environmental stimuli such as humidity and temperature, broadening their utility across diverse fields.
Micropatterning
Micropatterning techniques enable precise spatial control over material properties and surface functionalities. Using advanced methods like lithography, we fabricate microstructured surfaces that enhance optical transparency, mechanical stability, and environmental resilience. These patterned surfaces find applications in flexible electronics, optical devices, and multifunctional coatings that integrate hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions seamlessly.
Nanofibers
Electrospinning is a versatile technique for generating continuous nanofibers with high surface area, enhancing the wettability of materials. These nanofiber matrices exhibit a high surface area, interconnected pores, and thin permeation paths. By exploiting these properties, we aim to develop high-performance membranes with superior permeability for various applications.

tabs.label: Microfluidics
tabs.text:
Multi-phase Emulsion
Multi-phase emulsions, with their intricate structures, offer a platform where composition and structure can be precisely regulated through advanced microfluidic techniques. These systems enable independent control of inner and outer droplets, making them highly suitable for applications in sophisticated material encapsulation and controlled release. By leveraging diverse interfacial-active materials such as particles and surfactants, we fine-tune the physical and chemical properties of the emulsion shell, enabling selective material release and precise control over phase transitions. These emulsions are particularly promising as drug delivery systems and as microenvironments for catalytic reactions.
Vesicles and Microcapsules
Droplet microfluidics offers precise and simultaneous control over flow conditions, enabling the production of multiple emulsion droplets with tunable composition and structure. These droplets serve as versatile templates for incorporating unique functionalities tailored to specific applications. For instance, we utilize temperature-responsive materials in Janus particles to enhance emulsion stability while enabling on-demand coalescence. Additionally, we design shell membranes for double emulsion droplets and microcapsules to regulate material transport and utilize them in advanced smart release systems.
3D Printing
3D printing presents a groundbreaking approach to fabricating microfluidic devices, enabling the construction of microchannels with complex geometries. This technique allows for controlled outputs on the scale of tens of micrometers, facilitating the creation of fully three-dimensional channels and intricate surface modifications. Compared to traditional microfluidic fabrication methods, 3D printing enhances parallelization, screening capabilities, and mass production efficiency. It is widely applicable to various liquid-based processes, including micromixers, solution exchange, filtration, and droplet microfluidics.
Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)
Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is an indispensable tool for numerically analyzing and predicting fluid behavior, enabling the study of complex flow phenomena as well as thermal and mass transport across multiple scales. Our research leverages high-performance computing and diverse numerical methods to address challenges in fluid mechanics and uncover transformative insights. In real-world systems, multifaceted flow regimes—spanning laminar, turbulent, single-phase, and multiphase flows—frequently coexist. Through CFD simulations, we replicate these intricate dynamics with high fidelity, providing insights that are difficult to achieve experimentally. This approach improves predictive model reliability for design parameters such as flow distribution, pressure drops, temperature gradients, and concentration profiles. CFD also facilitates the transition from laboratory or pilot-scale verifications to full-scale commercial implementations by identifying and addressing latent flow issues, optimizing energy utilization, reaction efficiency, and production throughput. By integrating CFD, we aim to pioneer efficient and visionary fluid engineering solutions and foster cross-disciplinary innovation.

tabs.label: Encryption and Display
tabs.text:
Encryption and Display
Optical encryption technologies and dynamic displays are revolutionized through the integration of wettability patterning and structural color. By leveraging multi-level wettability systems and programmable photoreactive polymers, we create advanced anti-counterfeiting measures and transformational full-color devices. These innovations offer unprecedented control over color and information display, paving the way for secure, interactive, and visually striking solutions in information security and consumer electronics.

tabs.label: Artificial cell
tabs.text:
Artificial Cell
Cells perform a variety of complex biochemical reactions orchestrated in space and time. These features have driven advancements in biotechnology, biosensors, biogenesis, bioreactors, and drug delivery. To replicate and understand these cellular functions, we develop artificial cell-like vesicles that mimic key cellular hallmarks, including metabolic pathways, material transport, and protein synthesis. Using droplet microfluidics, we produce monodisperse vesicles with highly efficient encapsulation and compartmentalization of biomolecules. These artificial cells provide a new avenue for designing responsive and programmable protocell systems through a bottom-up approach.

tabs.label: Healthcare and Sustainability
tabs.text:
Healthcare and Sustainability
Conventional polymer materials are typically incinerated or landfilled, causing significant environmental and ecological harm. To address this, biodegradable materials have garnered considerable attention due to their ability to decompose into water and carbon dioxide through microbial activity. This environmentally friendly process eliminates the need for external energy inputs. Our research focuses on designing functional interfaces using these biodegradable materials, ensuring sustainability and contributing to environmental preservation.

Photocatalytic Nitrate Reduction
Overall water splitting with nanomaterials catalyst
Water splitting is a broad term referring to a chemical process where water is separated into oxygen and hydrogen. Efficient and cost-effective water splitting is crucial for the development of a hydrogen economy. Electrochemical water splitting, in particular, is recognized as the most promising technology for green hydrogen production. We are synthesizing nanomaterial electrode catalysts suitable for use in water electrolysis systems, employing various transition metals. Different synthesis methods, such as hydrothermal, thermal evaporation, chemical vapor deposition (CVD), and electrodeposition, are utilized to create transition metal compounds with diverse compositions, including hydroxides, phosphides, and sulfides. Furthermore, we have successfully integrated photovoltaic (PV) cells to establish self-powered electrochemical systems. A series-connected PV cell provides sufficient electrical power to drive electrochemical reactions. We have also developed a self-powered water electrolysis system that operates solely on solar energy by coupling the PV cell with the electrolysis cell, allowing for solar-driven water splitting. Reference papers: smll.201905501, D1TA01977E, D1TA02149D, apcatb.2021.120434
Hybrid water splitting
Overall water splitting involves the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) for hydrogen production and the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) for oxygen generation. Given its 4-electron process, the OER exhibits slow reactivity and demands relatively high overpotentials. To address these issues, we explore hybrid water splitting that substitute the OER with reactions like urea oxidation or hydrazine oxidation, which have lower theoretical potentials. These alternatives aim to enhance the efficiency of water splitting by addressing the sluggish kinetics and high overpotential associated with the OER. Reference paper: 154951, 155520, 4c00676
Membrane electrode assembly (MEA)
Conventional studies on water electrolysis have been conducted in batch systems with a lab-scale area ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 cm². However, the commercialization of green hydrogen production through water electrolysis requires the development of large-area cell systems utilizing Membrane Electrode Assemblies (MEA). MEA typically involves combining a large-area catalyst with proton exchange membranes, anion exchange membranes, bipolar membranes, and so on, to form the system. Our research specifically focuses on MEA systems that utilize anion exchange membranes, allowing for the utilization of non-precious metal catalysts. We are actively involved in exploring and advancing the application of non-precious metal catalysts in large-scale water electrolysis for efficient green hydrogen production. Reference paper: cej.2024.157106

Liquid-Solid triboelectric nanogenerator (L-S TENG)
Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert mechanical energy into electrical energy through triboelectrification and electrostatic induction, providing a renewable power source. While solid–solid TENGs are valued for their easy fabrication and low cost, liquid–solid (L-S) TENGs, especially water droplet-driven TENGs, offer advantages by harvesting energy from rain, rivers, and ocean waves. Expanding TENG applications requires intelligent low-power strategies, such as reversible switching of electrical output in response to external stimuli, enabling self-powered sensors and switches.
Our group has developed self-powered sensor systems based on L-S TENGs. We aim to optimize TENG performance by utilizing surface structure modifications and material property transitions in response to external stimuli, advancing them into sensor and energy conversion devices. Through this research, we seek practical applications in various fields, including smart sensors, wearable devices, and eco-friendly energy solutions.
Reference papers: DOI 2022, DOI 2024

tabs.label: Lithium-mediated Nitrogen Reduction
tabs.text:
Electrochemical Lithium-mediated Nitrogen Reduction Reaction (Li-NRR)
The Li-mediated Nitrogen Reduction Reaction (Li-NRR) literally refers to a process in which lithium mediates the reduction of nitrogen, ultimately aiming to synthesize ammonia. Ammonia, a key component in the production of fertilizers and various chemical industries, is the second most synthesized chemical in the world. Currently, the primary method for ammonia synthesis, the Haber-Bosch process, requires high temperatures of 350–450°C and high pressures of 150–200 atmospheres, resulting in approximately 1% of the world's energy being consumed solely for ammonia production. In contrast, Li-NRR can synthesize ammonia under ambient temperature and pressure, positioning it as a next-generation environmentally friendly green ammonia synthesis technology that could replace the Haber-Bosch process. We are conducting various studies to enhance the selectivity and conversion efficiency of Li-NRR.
Li-NRR fundamentally reduces nitrogen under non-aqueous conditions, and by altering various parameters such as the type of lithium salt, solvent, electrolyte additives, and electrodes, the selectivity and conversion efficiency of Li-NRR can be improved. These studies help identify factors that influence Li-NRR's selectivity and conversion efficiency, as well as uncover its mechanisms. For example, we have used dimethyl sulfide, a sulfur-containing compound, as an electrolyte additive to design the physicochemical structure of the solid-electrolyte interface (SEI), thereby achieving a steady cell potential. Through electrolyte modification, we have developed localized-high concentration electrolytes and steric hindrance-driven electrolytes, which form SEIs that are favorable for Li-NRR. These efforts have consistently enhanced the selectivity of Li-NRR and contributed significantly to the advancement of the field.
Reference papers: 3c02038,
202408280,
4c02626

tabs.label: Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction
tabs.text:
Electrochemical Nitrate Reduction Reaction (NORR)
The electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction (NORR) enables the sustainable synthesis of green ammonia by electrochemically reducing nitrate (NO₃⁻). Ammonia is the second most-produced chemical globally, primarily serving as a key precursor in fertilizers and chemical manufacturing. More recently, it has garnered attention as a hydrogen carrier due to its high hydrogen content and energy density. However, the conventional Haber-Bosch process operates under extreme temperature and pressure conditions, resulting in substantial CO₂ emissions and raising significant environmental concerns. To address these challenges, NORR has emerged as a promising alternative, utilizing nitrate from groundwater to contribute to pollution reduction while achieving high ammonia yield and excellent Faradaic efficiency. Compared to the nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR), NORR exhibits superior selectivity due to the favorable reduction properties of nitrogen oxides, establishing it as a viable pathway for renewable ammonia production.
We primarily focus on developing catalysts for NORR systems, synthesizing high-performance nanostructured catalysts using a variety of metals. In addition to utilizing equipment such as sputtering systems and furnaces, we employ diverse fabrication techniques, including electrodeposition, hydrothermal synthesis, and photodeposition, to optimize electrochemical catalyst performance. Furthermore, we investigate energy-efficient applications, including anodic coupling with alternative reactions and the assembly of Zn-nitrate batteries. From a systems perspective, we also strive to enhance the practical scalability of NORR by developing flow-based systems for large-scale ammonia production.

tabs.label: Solar Hydrogen Production
tabs.text:
Solar Hydrogen Production
Solar hydrogen production has been regarded as a key technology for solving the environmental issues because it utilizes two earth-abundant and clean sources, light and water. However, photocatalytic hydrogen production has a relatively low solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiency, due to the inefficient utilization of sunlight, charge recombination and sluggish kinetics of the surface reactions. Therefore, designing photocatalyst with broadened light absorption, enhanced charge carrier mobility and fastened reaction kinetics for hydrogen production is crucial in this field. To date, our group has investigated various particulate photocatalysts and photoelectrodes for solar hydrogen production.
Particulate Photocatalyst
Particulate photocatalyst is one of the simplest and cheapest method among the solar hydrogen production methods. However, the particle itself should have sufficient capability without external assistance. To enhance the efficiency of photocatalysts, we explored various catalytic engineering strategies such as cocatalyst deposition and heterojunction. Utilizing cocatalysts are one of the effective methods to facilitate the reaction kinetics because it can reduce activation energy of the process and serve as electron sink for enhanced charge separation. Typically, noble metals like Pt, Ru, and Au were employed. Furthermore, our group actively investigated heterojunction photocatalyst. The construction of heterostructure starts from attaching two types of semiconductor with unequal band structure. Our group focused on fabricating Z-scheme and type II heterojunction, which enabled efficient charge separation and enhanced light absorption, synergistically enhancing the overall solar-to-hydrogen efficiency.
Reference: Adv. Mater. 2023, 35, 2200172
Photoelectrochemical Cell (PEC)
In a PEC system, photoelectrodes are connected to charge collectors, providing extra potential needed for hydrogen production in addition to external power. Water is broken down into hydrogen and oxygen by electrolysis, but the electrical energy is obtained by a photoelectrochemical cell (PEC) process. The system is also named artificial photosynthesis. We have developed many types of PEC cells which consists of photoanode or photocathode and counter electrode. We developed metal oxides like ZnO, TiO2, WO3 as scaffold materials for photoanode, while BiVO4, CdS, CdSe are used to modify the surface of metal oxide scaffold. We studied charge transfer mechanism, doping analysis and co-catalysts to improve performance of the photoanode as well. Also, we investigated CIGS and p-Si for photocathode with non-noble metal co-catalyst, Ni-Mo.
Reference: Adv. Mater. 2017, 29, 1702431

tabs.label: Photocatalytic Nitrate Reduction
tabs.text:
Photocatalytic Nitrate (NO3-) Reduction to Ammonia (NH3) (PcNRA)
Ammonia (NH3) is indispensable chemical for its versatility in industrial and agricultural fields. Its usage has recently been extended as a carbon-free hydrogen carrier with its high hydrogen density. However, the conventional Haber-Bosch process has been criticized due to considerable amount of energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. Among the alternatives of environment-friendly ammonia production methods, photocatalytic nitrate (NO3-)-to-ammonia (PcNRA) is considered as an efficient strategy for green ammonia production. Moreover, NO3- is considered as organic pollutant in wastewater. Since PcNRA converts organic waste into value-added product, this can be a promising approach considering environmental concerns. There are two major pathways in photocatalytic nitrate reduction, nitrogen (N2) production and NH3 production. NO3—to-N2 pathway involves five electrons, while NO3--to-NH3 involves eight electrons. Additionally, the hydrogen evolution reaction involves only two electrons. Consequently, PcNRA has two kinetically favorable side reactions, which makes the primary purpose of this research to suppress the production of side products and enhance the NH3 selectivity. Our group has investigated efficient photocatalysts for PcNRA. We develop metal oxide-based catalysts like TiO2, SrTiO3 and organic semiconductors like g-C3N4. Our research specifically focuses on various catalytic engineering strategies like heteroatom doping, metal deposition and single atom catalysts. We actively work on developing photocatalysts for efficient and selective PcNRA.
Reference: Sol. RRL 2024, 8, 2300880

tabs.label: TENG
tabs.text:
Liquid-Solid triboelectric nanogenerator (L-S TENG)
Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert mechanical energy into electrical energy through triboelectrification and electrostatic induction, providing a renewable power source. While solid–solid TENGs are valued for their easy fabrication and low cost, liquid–solid (L-S) TENGs, especially water droplet-driven TENGs, offer advantages by harvesting energy from rain, rivers, and ocean waves. Expanding TENG applications requires intelligent low-power strategies, such as reversible switching of electrical output in response to external stimuli, enabling self-powered sensors and switches.
Our group has developed self-powered sensor systems based on L-S TENGs. We aim to optimize TENG performance by utilizing surface structure modifications and material property transitions in response to external stimuli, advancing them into sensor and energy conversion devices. Through this research, we seek practical applications in various fields, including smart sensors, wearable devices, and eco-friendly energy solutions.
Reference papers:
DOI 2022,
DOI 2024

tabs.label: ALD
tabs.text:
Next Generation Semiconductor Device Processing
Atomic layer deposition
Atomic Layer Chemical Vapor Deposition(ALCVD) is vapor deposition method, which precursor and reactant are injected in the reactor alternatively. Different from normal MOCVD process, it is self-limited surface reaction which is affected by the surface temperature. Monolayer of material is deposited by repeated exposure of precursor and reactant. ALCVD process is a key process in the fabrication of semiconductor device because of these deposition characteristics.
Oxygen diffusion blocking layer (ODBL)
In atomic layer deposition (ALD) of high-k materials, an oxygen diffusion blocking layer is essential to prevent unwanted oxygen penetration, which can degrade interface quality and electrical performance. This layer acts as a barrier, maintaining the desired stoichiometry of the high-k film and preventing oxidation-induced defects in the underlying substrate. Effective blocking layers, such as metal nitrides or oxides, enhance device reliability and electrical stability, making them crucial for high-performance electronic applications.
Reference papers:
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsf.2020.138368

Research Topic 1: Sustainable Biorefinery with Process Design and Systems-level Analysis
Research Goal (연구 목표): 미활용 바이오매스 유래 전 공정 모사 및 모니터링 플랫폼 기술 개발
Our group's research goal is to create a systematic method for sustainable energy process systems design by incorporating various theories and techniques of process systems engineering area and developing a sustainable (economic, low environmental impact, low waste, efficient operation, correct raw material) process flowsheet that can convert the raw materials to the desired products. Its applications that we have been focusing on are synthesis of biomass-to-fuels/Chemicals and CO2&H2-to-fuels/chemicals.

Research Topic 2 : Waste Materials Recycling with Process Design
Research Goal (연구 목표): 폐 자원으로부터 고부가가치 물질을 회수하기 위한 공정 모사 및 경제 환경적 실현 가능성 분석 플랫폼 개발
Our research group's goal is to develop a systematic approach to designing sustainable energy process systems by integrating various process systems engineering theories and techniques. To achieve this, we aim to develop an environmentally friendly process flow for recovering valuable materials from waste resources. areas.name: Research Topic3
areas.text:
Research Topic 3 : Renewable energy with Process Simulation and LCA/TEA
Research Goal (연구 목표): 재생에너지 기반 공정모사를 통한 친환경 에너지 기술의 실현 가능성 및 지속가능성 평가 플랫폼 개발
Our research goal is to develop a systematic evaluation and design framework for renewable energy technologies by integrating process simulation with life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA). This framework aims to assess the environmental and economic feasibility of renewable energy production processes, including electricity- and hydrogen-based systems, as well as emerging clean energy technologies. In particular, our research focuses on (i) the development and assessment of environmentally friendly processes for renewable energy production, (ii) the design and evaluation of perovskite solar cell (PSC) fabrication and recycling processes using biomass-derived green solvents, and (iii) the modeling, analysis, and optimization of carbon capture and utilization (CCU) pathways based on CO₂ reduction potential and economic performance.

areas.name: Research Topic4
areas.text:
Research Topic 4 : Carbon Capture and Utilization with Process Simulation and Optimization
Research Goal (연구 목표): 수소/CCUS 기술의 상용화를 위한 최적 설계 방법론 개발 및 실증 규모 공정 개선
Our group's research goal is to minimize cost, maximize throughput, and/or efficiency of a process, while keeping its constraints satisfied. Its applications that we have been focusing on are optimization-based assessment frameworks for large scale CCUS (CO2 capture and utilization/storage) infrastructure design and large scale renewable energy (H2) supply chain management.
Modeling of unit operations: H2/CO2 분리, 전환 공정 등 다양한 H2/CCUS 제반 공정 기술 개발
Process integration: H2/CCUS 요소 기술간 및 기존 상용 공정과의 통합 전략 수립
Supply chain network design: 상부구조시스템(superstructure) 기반의 H2/CCU 통합 시스템에 대한 경제성 및 CO2 저감량 분석 및 극대화를 위한 개별 공정 최적화
Scenario-based analysis: 다양한 시나리오 (탄소 감축 및 중립 포트폴리오 등) 기반의 최적 H2/CCUS technology platform 분석

areas.name: Research Topic 5
areas.text:
Research Topic 5 : Data Prediction with Artificial Intelligence and Mathematical Modeling
Research Goal (연구 목표): 인공지능 및 수학적 모델링 기반 데이터 예측 기법을 통한 공정·소재·에너지 시스템 성능의 정량적 예측
We aim to develop data-driven prediction frameworks by integrating artificial intelligence with mathematical modeling to enhance process and system-level decision-making. Our research focuses on building data platforms for materials and process design, as well as developing machine-learning models for property prediction based on molecular representations. In particular, we target applications such as intelligent semiconductor device design and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) property prediction, enabling standards compliance assessment and optimal pathway through AI-assisted analysis.

areas.name: Research Topic 6
areas.text:
Research Topic 6: New Energy Technologies with Process Optimization and Dynamic Modeling
Research Goal (연구 목표): 차세대 에너지 기술 대상 공정 최적화와 정적·동적 모사를 결합한 시스템 수준 분석
We aim to develop system-level modeling and optimization frameworks for new energy technologies by integrating process design, dynamic modeling, and advanced optimization techniques. Our research focuses on catalytic and CCU-based chemical production processes, integrated LNG–SOFC–CCUS systems, and fusion energy fuel cycle technologies, including detritiation systems. Through steady-state and dynamic simulation, as well as data-driven surrogate modeling, we seek to enhance process efficiency, controllability, and environmental performance of emerging energy systems.
