overview:
Smart nanoparticle for drug delivery system
Drug delivery system is a powerful technology to increase the efficacy of drugs and reduc
e the side effects by loading the drug in the specific carriers and accumulating them at s
pecific area. Our group has developed various carriers such as polymeric nanoparticles, g
old nanoparticles, mesoporous silica nanoparticles, and polymeric micelles, etc. In additio
n, various functionalities has been introduced to the carrier; for instance, carriers can relea
se cargos in response to light, reactive oxygen species, pH, intracellular reducing environ
ment, or generate reactive oxygen species and heat by irradiation of light or ultrasound.
To transport the synthesized carriers to specific tissues more efficiently, targeting ligands
including antibodies, aptamers and peptides can be introduced on the surface of the c
arriers. Our smart drug delivery carriers show higher efficacy than conventional drugs in t
he treatment of various incurable diseases, and our final goal is conquest of various disea
ses.

areas.name: Gene delivery
areas.text:
Gene delivery using biomedical polymer
Gene delivery is introducing nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA into target cells to correct defective genes which induce disease. Generally, the correction is achieved through
1) introducing lacking genetic materials,
2) blocking mutated genes
3) replacing the mutated genes with normal genes
Our group has developed a variety of polymer based and hybrid gene delivery carrier utilizing cationic polymer, inorganic materials and even nucleic acids in order to protect the genes from enzymes or damages and facilitate uptake of the genes into the target cells. Furthermore, various chemical bonds which could be cleaved at specific stimuli have been introduced for more effective gene delivery: pH, reducing environment and bio-molecules including ATP, sugar and nucleic acids have been applied. As well, targeting moieties have been conjugated with the carrier for specific tumor-targeting. Those strategies provide highly effective and specific gene delivery, and we have used the strategies for developing novel gene delivery carrier as our research goal.

areas.name: Cancer immunotherapy
areas.text:
Cancer immunotherapy using nanoparticle
Cancer immunotherapy (CIT), harnessing the immune system to induce the death of cancer cells or alter the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, has been extensively investigated due to its therapeutic potential. Despite its promising potential, instability of immunomodulators, systemic adverse effect, and resulting insufficient immunogenicity remain as barriers. Our major goal of research is to design of nanomaterial-based strategies that enhance the efficiency and efficacy of immunomodulators. Introduction of nanomaterials into immumotherapy enables stable delivery of immunomodulators with spatiotemporal-specific release as well as combinatorial therapy with the existing cancer therapy methods including chemotherapy, photothermal therapy, and photodynamic therapy. Recently, we are studying the site-specific immunomodulator delivery using tumor microenvironment and combination of immunotherapy with developed nanomedicine. Our novel strategies would suggest new perspectives for breakthrough of current immunotherapy.

areas.name: NO related materials
areas.text:
Nitric Oxide related materials
Nitric Oxide (NO)-related therapeutics is a rising research field, because NO has intrinsic physiological effects such as neurotransmitter, immune regulator and vasodilator etc. However, due to the short life time of NO radical molecule, introducing NO donor is needed for delivering NO to human body. Our group has applied various biocompatible NO donor for antibacterial effects, antitumor effects, vasodilation, wound healing effects and BBB opening effects. Furthermore, stimuli responsive NO delivery system also has developed, such as ultrasound, high intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) and pH to enhance therapeutic effect and reduce side effects. However, if NO is overproduced by physiological disorders, it can lead to severe inflammatory diseases including rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and bowel disease etc. For treating these disease, we also researches NO-responsiveness and try to extend NO-scavenging materials as therapeutics such as NO-responsive hydrogel and NO-scavenging nanogel. We believed that our novel materials have a potential as a therapeutic material for various incurable and inflammatory disorders.

areas.name: DNA engineering
areas.text:
DNA engineering for various diseases therapeutics
DNA engineering is becoming an attractive research area due to the high potential of DNA as a material. High programmability, predictability, and biocompatibility promise the DNA as an excellent biomaterial for biomedical applications. Our group has been developed various DNA based systems for SNP detection, small molecule detection, protein capture, and therapeutics. Detection or sensing systems were developed based on the change of base pairing upon different conditions. Meanwhile, protein capture systems or therapeutic systems were developed using the aptamers which are able to target specific protein. In addition, conjugation of DNA on polymers or other materials widen the stability or functionallity of oligonucleotides, improved our systems. Our DNA engineering and DNA based systems show impressive effect on detection, sensing, capture, and therapeutics. We expect our technology will be expanded to various biological systems that other materials can not achieve.

Our Vision
The Nanotrio refers to a class of diverse nanomaterials developed at the intersection of nanophotonics, nanoplasmonics, and nanobiotechnology. Our research explores the synthesis, characterization, and potential applications of nanomaterials, with a particular focus on quantum dots, plasmonic nanoparticles, and nanocomposites with tunable morphologies and sophisticated nanostructures.
We specialize in characterizing the “small world” of nanomaterials using absorption and emission spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, dynamic light scattering, and zeta-potential analysis. Through these analyses, we investigate the properties of synthesized materials and use the resulting insights to guide the future design of functional nanomaterials.
Our goal is to understand the unique physical properties of nanomaterials and translate them into practical applications in nanotherapy, nanoenergy, nanodiagnostics, and other emerging fields.
Ongoing Research Projects (For more information, please visit the Project page)
Our Nanotrio laboratory conducts research in nanoscience and nanobiology, focusing on the interaction between light and matter at the nanoscale. We study the synthesis, surface control, assembly, and complexation of nanocrystals to develop nanostructures and advanced materials with potential applications in displays, photodetectors, photovoltaics, photoelectrochemical cells, sensors, and bioimaging. In particular, we study semiconductor nanocrystals, such as quantum dots and QLED materials, as well as nanostructured materials based on gold nanoparticles that can be used for sensing and three-dimensional cell imaging. By leveraging the unique physical properties of nanomaterials, we aim to develop functional materials for a wide range of optical, electronic, and biomedical applications.
We synthesize new nanocrystals by controlling precursor reactivity and reaction intermediates. Quantum dots are inorganic nanocrystals with a molecular-level size distribution, and their small size allows a large number of atoms to reside at the surface. For example, InP quantum dots, which are widely used in QLED displays, can contain approximately 1,000 to 10,000 atoms, depending on the size. Although the exact atomic structure and growth mechanism of these nanocrystals remain difficult to determine, quantized intermediates can form during their synthesis. These intermediates are structurally analogous to the critical nuclei described in classical nucleation theory. Our research focuses on understanding these intermediate nanoclusters and controlling their formation through precursor chemistry, with the goal of establishing growth pathways and mechanistic principles for the development of high-performance QLED nanocrystals.
We also investigate surface chemistry at the nanoscale. Surface chemistry is essential for forming efficient conjugates with proteins, DNA, and antibodies, and it plays a critical role in controlling colloidal stability and surface functionality. In particular, we study ultrafast surface modification using quantized ions and investigate reversible surface bonding based on hydrogen-bonding interactions. Through these approaches, we aim to establish precise and efficient strategies for tailoring nanocrystal surfaces.
Another major focus of our research is near-infrared optical materials. Compared with conventional molecular or organic materials, quantum dots can emit in the near-infrared region while exhibiting high photostability and size-tunable optical properties. Quantum-dot-based optical probes can also be miniaturized and used for ultrahigh-sensitivity sensing through solution-based processes such as inkjet printing. Using these properties, we develop new near-infrared fluorescent probes and materials. In addition, we are developing brain–computer interfaces that use autonomous quantum-dot probes to visualize real-time physiological signals in the brain, thereby enabling new approaches for understanding human cognition and neural activity. We are also synthesizing biocompatible nanocrystals and converting them into oil-in-fluorocarbon materials for biomedical applications.
We develop nanorobotic probes that respond to environmental stimuli, such as pH, by changing their optical properties. Like cuttlefish that change color in response to their surroundings, these nanorobotic probes are designed to alter their optical signals when exposed to specific environments. Quantum-dot optical probes can also be used as next-generation display materials because they provide a wide color gamut and can respond sensitively to external stimuli. By programming their response to specific conditions, these probes can visualize changes that are difficult to detect directly. For example, quantum dots that respond to magnetic field variations are being investigated as magnetoplasmonic nanorobot probes that use gold nanoparticles and can be applied to next-generation transparent displays, including AR and VR technologies.
Finally, we are developing barcode technologies using near-infrared probes to overcome the limitations of conventional molecular probes and to enable simultaneous detection of multiple targets. Because of their strong photostability, high brightness, and narrow emission bandwidth, quantum dots can provide highly multiplexed optical signals. Antibody–quantum dot conjugates can be used for rapid and quantitative target detection in complex biological environments. These nanomaterials offer advantages for medical diagnosis, bioimaging, and precision sensing by minimizing biological background interference and providing distinct multicolor optical signals. Through this research, we aim to develop quantum-dot-based molecular barcode platforms capable of detecting multiple professional-level diagnostic signals simultaneously.

매직 크기 나노클러스터 합성
마직 크기 나노클러스터(MSC)는 분자 전구체와 콜로이드 양자점 사이의 중간 단계에 해당하는 나노 구조체입니다. MSC는 수백 개 이하의 원자로 구성된 3 nm 미만의 극소 크기임에도 불구하고, 동일한 크기의 일반 나노입자보다 열역학적으로 높은 안정성을 나타내는 것이 가장 큰 특징입니다. 흡수 스펙트럼에서 특정 파장에 고정된 선명한 흡수 피크가 나타나는 것도 MSC를 구별하는 중요한 지표이며, 이러한 특성을 바탕으로 비고전적 합성 경로를 통해 다양한 나노소재를 제조하기 위한 전구체로서의 활용 가능성이 주목받고 있습니다. 본 연구팀은 MSC의 합성, 분리 및 물성 규명 연구를 수행하고 있으며, 나아가 MSC가 갖는 독특한 광학적 특성에도 주목하고 있습니다. 특히 정이십면체 구조를 갖는 MSC는 라세미 혼합물 형태로 존재하며, 리간드를 이용한 분리 또는 키랄 컬럼 크로마토그래피를 통해 좌우 거울상 이성질체로 분리될 수 있습니다. 이러한 키랄 MSC는 원편광이색성(CD) 스펙트럼에서 거울 대칭의 신호를 나타내는 등 특이한 광학 활성을 보이며, 이를 통해 MSC의 구조와 광특성 사이의 관계를 탐구하는 연구를 진행하고 있습니다.

양자점-고분자 복합 콜로이드 플랫폼을 활용한 바이오센싱 및 생체 이미징
양자점은 높은 광안정성과 조성에 따라 조절 가능한 발광 특성 덕분에 생체 환경에서의 신호 측정 및 이미징에 유망한 소재입니다. 본 연구팀은 양친매성 폴리에틸렌이민(amPEI)을 기반으로 수십 개의 양자점을 단일 나노입자 내에 캡슐화한 복합 콜로이드(QDCC) 플랫폼을 개발하고, 이를 다양한 바이오 응용으로 확장하는 연구를 수행하고 있습니다. 복합 콜로이드의 외부에 고분자 전해질 다층막(layer-by-layer, LbL)을 순차적으로 코팅하면 구조적 견고성과 투과성을 세밀하게 조절할 수 있으며, 표면에 쯔비터이온 작용기를 도입함으로써 넓은 pH 범위와 고농도 염 조건에서도 우수한 콜로이드 안정성을 확보할 수 있습니다. 이를 기반으로 생체 내 표적 단백질에 대한 면역분석 시스템을 구축하고, 생물학적 자기조립을 통한 신호 증폭 전략을 적용하여 극미량의 바이오마커를 빠르게 검출하는 플랫폼으로 발전시키고 있습니다. 또한 amPEI의 유연한 내부 구조는 기체 분자가 쉽게 드나들 수 있어, 산화질소(NO)와 같은 생리활성 기체 분자에 반응하는 물질을 양자점과 함께 캡슐화하여 비율측정형(ratiometric) 센서로 활용하는 연구도 진행하고 있습니다. 이 플랫폼은 세포 내 산소 농도 모니터링, 산화질소 실시간 검출 등 다양한 생체 환경 측정에 적용 가능한 범용 나노센서 플랫폼으로 자리매김할 수 있을 것으로 기대됩니다.

금 나노입자는 나노미터 크기에서 독특한 표면 플라즈몬 공명 특성을 나타내며, 입자 간 거리와 배열에 따라 광학적 특성이 크게 달라집니다. 본 연구팀은 금 나노입자의 표면에 외부 자극에 반응하는 리간드를 설계하여, pH 변화나 산화-환원 반응과 같은 화학적 신호에 의해 입자의 분산과 응집을 가역적으로 제어하는 연구를 수행하고 있습니다. 리간드가 외부 자극에 반응하면 입자 간 상호작용과 플라즈모닉 커플링이 변화하고, 이에 따라 나노입자 집합체의 광학적 특성이 가역적으로 조절됩니다. 이러한 접근은 나노입자의 콜로이드 안정성, 조립 거동, 그리고 자극 의존적 광 반응을 정밀하게 제어할 수 있는 플랫폼을 제공합니다. 이를 기반으로 암 광열 치료, 광음향 이미징, 암세포 선택적 약물 전달 등 다양한 의생명 응용 연구를 진행하고 있습니다. 나아가 최근에는 전기화학적 자극에 의해 금속-리간드 배위 결합이 가역적으로 형성되고 끊어지는 현상을 활용하여, 입자 간 플라즈모닉 커플링을 전기적으로 제어하는 재구성 가능한 광학 소재 및 스마트 센싱 플랫폼 개발로 연구를 확장하고 있습니다.
Project Period
2022.02.28~2027.02.28
Funding Agency
Host Institution
6
나노결정 표면 화학 제어
나노결정의 성능은 내부 결정 구조만큼이나 표면에서 일어나는 원자 수준의 상호작용에 의해 결정됩니다. 본 연구팀은 은 칼코게나이드 나노결정을 중심으로, 표면 원자의 종류와 리간드 결합 환경이 나노결정의 광학적 특성과 화학적 안정성에 어떤 영향을 미치는지 체계적으로 연구하고 있습니다. 나노결정 표면에는 결정 격자 내부에 속한 원자와 격자 경계 바깥에 노출된 원자가 공존하며, 이 두 종류의 원자는 서로 다른 리간드 결합 특성을 나타냅니다. 본 연구팀은 이러한 표면 위치별 결합 특성의 차이를 규명하고, 이를 활용하여 나노결정을 안정적으로 패시베이션하는 전략을 개발하고 있습니다. 이를 통해 나노결정의 융합과 형태 변형 없이 양이온 교환이나 코어-껍질 구조 형성 같은 후속 화학 반응을 정밀하게 수행할 수 있습니다. 또한 표면에 존재하는 원자의 종류와 비율을 조절하면 나노결정 내 전하 트랩 특성을 원하는 방향으로 설계할 수 있다는 점에 주목하여, 이를 광검출 소자 등 실제 응용으로 연결하는 연구도 진행하고 있습니다.

5
양이온 교환을 통한 나노결정 조성 및 형태 제어
양이온 교환 반응은 음이온 격자를 유지한 채 양이온만을 선택적으로 치환하는 합성 전략입니다. 입자의 형태와 크기를 보존하면서도 조성을 자유롭게 바꿀 수 있어, 단일 전구체에서 다양한 합금 나노결정을 만들어내는 강력한 도구입니다. 본 연구팀은 전구체의 반응성을 정밀하게 설계함으로써 이 교환 반응의 경로를 원하는 단계에서 정확히 멈추는 방법을 개발하고 있습니다. (1) 반응성 제어 전구체를 이용한 Ag-Au-S 양자점의 단계별 양이온 교환 기존 방법으로 Ag₂S 양자점에 금을 도입하면 조성이 불균일한 혼합물이 생성되어 발광 스펙트럼이 넓어지는 문제가 있었습니다. 본 연구에서는 금 전구체의 반응성을 리간드 배위, 금속 간 결합, 입체 효과를 통해 단계적으로 낮춤으로써, Ag₃AuS₂ 및 AgAuS 양자점을 높은 상순도로 선택적으로 합성하는 데 성공하였습니다. 이를 통해 적색~근적외선 영역(663–1192 nm)에 걸쳐 좁고 밝은 발광 특성을 구현하였으며, 전구체 반응성 설계가 합금 나노결정 합성의 핵심 원리임을 제시하였습니다. (2) 형태 보존 양이온 교환을 통한 나노결정 설계 양이온 교환 반응에서 음이온 골격이 유지되는 특성을 활용하면, 입자의 형태와 구조적 특징을 그대로 보존하면서 조성만을 유연하게 바꿀 수 있습니다. 이 접근법은 두 가지 이상의 금속 성분을 포함하는 합금 나노구조체의 합성으로도 확장 가능하며, 기존 직접 합성으로는 구현하기 어려운 다양한 조성의 나노결정을 체계적으로 설계하는 플랫폼으로 활용됩니다.
Project Period
2022.03.01~2027.02.28
Funding Agency
Host Institution
4
차세대 디스플레이를 위한 청색 발광 소재 개발
스마트폰과 TV 디스플레이의 선명한 색을 구현하는 핵심 소재인 양자점은 나노미터 수준의 크기 제어만으로 발광 색을 자유롭게 조절할 수 있는 차세대 발광 재료입니다. 본 연구팀은 친환경 차세대 디스플레이 실현을 위해 아직 상용화되지 못한 난제, 고성능 청색 양자점 소재 개발에 도전하고 있습니다. 우리 연구실만의 독자적인 접근법은 나노클러스터를 전구체로 활용하는 것입니다. 원자 수준에서 구조와 조성이 정밀하게 정의된 나노클러스터를 출발 재료로 사용함으로써, 기존 방법으로는 제어하기 어려웠던 양자점의 성장 과정을 처음 단계부터 정교하게 조절합니다. 이를 통해 색순도와 발광 효율이 동시에 우수한 청색 양자점 합성을 목표로 합니다. 나아가 점 형태의 양자점을 넘어, 1차원 나노막대 합성 연구도 진행하고 있습니다. 나노막대가 가지는 편광 발광 특성은 기존 발광 소자의 효율 한계를 뛰어넘을 수 있는 가능성을 열어줍니다.

tabs.text:
Our Vision
The Nanotrio refers to a class of diverse nanomaterials developed at the intersection of nanophotonics, nanoplasmonics, and nanobiotechnology. Our research explores the synthesis, characterization, and potential applications of nanomaterials, with a particular focus on quantum dots, plasmonic nanoparticles, and nanocomposites with tunable morphologies and sophisticated nanostructures.
We specialize in characterizing the “small world” of nanomaterials using absorption and emission spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, dynamic light scattering, and zeta-potential analysis. Through these analyses, we investigate the properties of synthesized materials and use the resulting insights to guide the future design of functional nanomaterials.
Our goal is to understand the unique physical properties of nanomaterials and translate them into practical applications in nanotherapy, nanoenergy, nanodiagnostics, and other emerging fields.
Ongoing Research Projects (For more information, please visit the Project page)
Our Nanotrio laboratory conducts research in nanoscience and nanobiology, focusing on the interaction between light and matter at the nanoscale. We study the synthesis, surface control, assembly, and complexation of nanocrystals to develop nanostructures and advanced materials with potential applications in displays, photodetectors, photovoltaics, photoelectrochemical cells, sensors, and bioimaging. In particular, we study semiconductor nanocrystals, such as quantum dots and QLED materials, as well as nanostructured materials based on gold nanoparticles that can be used for sensing and three-dimensional cell imaging. By leveraging the unique physical properties of nanomaterials, we aim to develop functional materials for a wide range of optical, electronic, and biomedical applications.
We synthesize new nanocrystals by controlling precursor reactivity and reaction intermediates. Quantum dots are inorganic nanocrystals with a molecular-level size distribution, and their small size allows a large number of atoms to reside at the surface. For example, InP quantum dots, which are widely used in QLED displays, can contain approximately 1,000 to 10,000 atoms, depending on the size. Although the exact atomic structure and growth mechanism of these nanocrystals remain difficult to determine, quantized intermediates can form during their synthesis. These intermediates are structurally analogous to the critical nuclei described in classical nucleation theory. Our research focuses on understanding these intermediate nanoclusters and controlling their formation through precursor chemistry, with the goal of establishing growth pathways and mechanistic principles for the development of high-performance QLED nanocrystals.
We also investigate surface chemistry at the nanoscale. Surface chemistry is essential for forming efficient conjugates with proteins, DNA, and antibodies, and it plays a critical role in controlling colloidal stability and surface functionality. In particular, we study ultrafast surface modification using quantized ions and investigate reversible surface bonding based on hydrogen-bonding interactions. Through these approaches, we aim to establish precise and efficient strategies for tailoring nanocrystal surfaces.
Another major focus of our research is near-infrared optical materials. Compared with conventional molecular or organic materials, quantum dots can emit in the near-infrared region while exhibiting high photostability and size-tunable optical properties. Quantum-dot-based optical probes can also be miniaturized and used for ultrahigh-sensitivity sensing through solution-based processes such as inkjet printing. Using these properties, we develop new near-infrared fluorescent probes and materials. In addition, we are developing brain–computer interfaces that use autonomous quantum-dot probes to visualize real-time physiological signals in the brain, thereby enabling new approaches for understanding human cognition and neural activity. We are also synthesizing biocompatible nanocrystals and converting them into oil-in-fluorocarbon materials for biomedical applications.
We develop nanorobotic probes that respond to environmental stimuli, such as pH, by changing their optical properties. Like cuttlefish that change color in response to their surroundings, these nanorobotic probes are designed to alter their optical signals when exposed to specific environments. Quantum-dot optical probes can also be used as next-generation display materials because they provide a wide color gamut and can respond sensitively to external stimuli. By programming their response to specific conditions, these probes can visualize changes that are difficult to detect directly. For example, quantum dots that respond to magnetic field variations are being investigated as magnetoplasmonic nanorobot probes that use gold nanoparticles and can be applied to next-generation transparent displays, including AR and VR technologies.
Finally, we are developing barcode technologies using near-infrared probes to overcome the limitations of conventional molecular probes and to enable simultaneous detection of multiple targets. Because of their strong photostability, high brightness, and narrow emission bandwidth, quantum dots can provide highly multiplexed optical signals. Antibody–quantum dot conjugates can be used for rapid and quantitative target detection in complex biological environments. These nanomaterials offer advantages for medical diagnosis, bioimaging, and precision sensing by minimizing biological background interference and providing distinct multicolor optical signals. Through this research, we aim to develop quantum-dot-based molecular barcode platforms capable of detecting multiple professional-level diagnostic signals simultaneously.

진행 중인 연구 분야
● 나노트리오 연구실은 나노스케일에서 빛과 물질의 상호작용을 이해하고 제어하는 것을 목표로, 나노과학 및 나노바이오 분야의 연구를 수행하고 있습니다. 본 연구실은 나노결정의 합성, 표면 제어, 조립 및 복합화 연구를 통해 디스플레이, 광검출기, 태양전지, 광전기화학 소자, 센서, 바이오이미징 등 다양한 분야에 활용될 수 있는 나노구조체와 첨단 소재를 개발하고 있습니다. 특히 양자점 및 QLED 소재로 활용되는 반도체 나노결정과, 센싱 및 3차원 세포 이미징에 적용 가능한 금 나노입자 기반 나노구조체를 중점적으로 연구하고 있습니다. 이를 통해 나노소재 고유의 물리적 특성을 활용하여 광학, 전자, 바이오의학 분야에서 기능성 소재로 발전시키는 것을 목표로 합니다.
● 본 연구실은 전구체의 반응성과 반응 중간체를 제어함으로써 새로운 나노결정을 합성하는 연구를 수행하고 있습니다. 양자점은 분자 수준의 크기 분포를 갖는 무기 나노결정으로, 매우 작은 크기 때문에 많은 수의 원자가 표면에 존재합니다. 예를 들어 QLED 디스플레이에 널리 사용되는 InP 양자점은 크기에 따라 약 1,000개에서 10,000개의 원자로 구성될 수 있습니다. 이러한 나노결정은 정확한 원자 구조와 성장 메커니즘을 규명하기 어렵지만, 합성 과정에서 양자화된 중간체가 형성될 수 있습니다. 이러한 중간체는 고전적 핵생성 이론에서 설명하는 임계핵과 구조적으로 유사한 나노클러스터로 볼 수 있습니다. 본 연구실은 이러한 중간 나노클러스터의 형성과 반응성을 이해하고, 전구체 화학을 통해 이를 제어함으로써 고성능 QLED 나노결정 개발을 위한 성장 경로와 성장 원리를 확립하고자 합니다.
● 또한 나노스케일에서의 표면화학을 연구하고 있습니다. 표면화학은 단백질, DNA, 항체 등과의 효율적인 결합체 형성에 필수적이며, 콜로이드 안정성과 표면 기능성을 조절하는 데 중요한 역할을 합니다. 특히 본 연구실은 양자화된 이온을 이용한 초고속 표면 개질과 수소결합 상호작용을 기반으로 한 가역적 표면 결합을 연구하고 있습니다. 이러한 접근을 통해 나노결정 표면을 정밀하고 효율적으로 조절할 수 있는 전략을 확립하고자 합니다.
● 다른 주요 연구 주제는 근적외선 광학 소재입니다. 일반적인 분자 또는 유기 소재와 비교할 때, 양자점은 높은 광안정성과 크기 조절이 가능한 광학 특성을 가지면서 근적외선 영역에서 발광할 수 있습니다. 또한 양자점 기반 광학 프로브는 소형화가 가능하고, 잉크젯 프린팅과 같은 용액 공정을 통해 초고감도 센싱 플랫폼으로 활용될 수 있습니다. 본 연구실은 이러한 특성을 활용하여 새로운 근적외선 형광 프로브와 소재를 개발하고 있습니다. 더 나아가, 자율적으로 작동하는 양자점 프로브를 통해 뇌의 생리적 신호를 실시간으로 시각화하고, 이를 기반으로 인간의 인지 및 신경 활동을 이해하기 위한 뇌-컴퓨터 인터페이스 기술을 개발하고 있습니다. 또한 생체적합성 나노결정을 합성하고 이를 오일-인-플루오로카본 소재로 전환하여 바이오의학 응용으로 확장하는 연구도 수행하고 있습니다.
● pH와 같은 환경 자극에 반응하여 광학 특성이 변화하는 나노로봇 프로브를 개발하고 있습니다. 주변 환경에 따라 색을 변화시키는 갑오징어처럼, 이러한 나노로봇 프로브는 특정 환경에 노출되었을 때 광학 신호가 변화하도록 설계됩니다. 양자점 기반 광학 프로브는 넓은 색 영역을 구현할 수 있고 외부 자극에 민감하게 반응할 수 있어 차세대 디스플레이 소재로도 활용될 수 있습니다. 특정 조건에 반응하도록 프로그래밍된 프로브는 직접 관찰하기 어려운 변화를 시각화할 수 있습니다. 예를 들어 자기장 변화에 반응하는 양자점은 금 나노입자를 이용한 자기-플라즈몬 나노로봇 프로브로 연구되고 있으며, AR/VR 기술과 같은 차세대 투명 디스플레이 응용으로 확장될 수 있습니다.
● 마지막으로, 기존 분자 프로브의 한계를 극복하고 여러 표적을 동시에 검출하기 위해 근적외선 프로브 기반 바코드 기술을 개발하고 있습니다. 양자점은 높은 광안정성, 강한 발광 세기, 좁은 발광 대역폭을 가지므로 다중화된 광학 신호를 제공할 수 있습니다. 항체–양자점 접합체는 복잡한 생물학적 환경에서도 표적을 빠르고 정량적으로 검출하는 데 활용될 수 있습니다. 이러한 나노소재는 생체 배경 신호의 간섭을 줄이고, 서로 구분 가능한 다색 광학 신호를 제공함으로써 의료 진단, 바이오이미징, 정밀 센싱 분야에서 장점을 가집니다. 본 연구실은 이러한 연구를 통해 여러 진단 신호를 동시에 검출할 수 있는 양자점 기반 분자 바코드 플랫폼을 개발하고자 합니다.

tabs.label: Nanophotonics
tabs.text:
Nanophotonics
The emission wavelength and intensity of QDs can be precisely controlled, making them versatile materials for switchable probes in cellular and whole-body imaging, optical modulation, and light-emitting devices. Our group synthesizes a wide range of nanomaterials, including core/shell QDs, nanorods, nanotetrapods, and nanoporous structures. We have demonstrated the photomodulation of QD conjugates using additional UV excitation, which promotes electron transfer to the QDs and quenches their photoluminescence. We have also developed inorganic-ligand-capped QDs as sensitizers for solar-cell applications.
1. Optical properties of quantum dots
Semiconductor nanocrystals, commonly referred to as quantum dots (QDs), differ from bulk semiconductors in that their optical properties are strongly dependent on size. In semiconductor nanocrystals with diameters of only a few nanometers, electrons and holes are confined within a space smaller than the exciton Bohr radius, giving rise to quantum confinement in all three dimensions. This confinement produces discrete electronic energy levels and makes the band gap (BG) between the valence band and the conduction band dependent on nanocrystal size. The BG determines the energy required for photoexcitation and the subsequent radiative relaxation process. As the size of a QD decreases, the BG increases, leading to absorption and fluorescence at shorter wavelengths (Fig. 1). QD core/shell structure can be classified into type-I and type-II (Fig. 2)
Semiconductor QDs can be categorized into type-I and type-II structures according to their band alignment. In type-I QDs, the shell material has a larger BG than the core material, allowing the electron–hole pair to be confined within the core. This confinement enhances photoluminescence (PL) efficiency, making type-I QDs useful for highly emissive applications. In type-II QDs, the valence and conduction band edges of the core and shell are staggered, which spatially separates electrons and holes across the core/shell interface (Fig. 3a). This charge separation makes type-II QDs attractive for energy-conversion applications, including solar cells. Changes in the valence and conduction band alignment of the core and shell alter the spatial distribution of electron and hole densities. This band engineering also creates an effective BG that is not determined solely by the intrinsic band gaps of the constituent materials, enabling control over both absorption and PL wavelengths (Fig. 3).
Colloidal nanocrystals synthesized from solution-phase precursors offer broad tunability in morphology and size, providing many opportunities for functional applications. Morphological control is important because nanocrystal shape and internal structure influence electronic energy states, charge-carrier mobility, and exciton localization. These morphologies can be controlled by regulating nucleation and growth processes from the atomic level. Such processes are governed by both kinetic factors, including reactant concentration and diffusion, and thermodynamic factors, including surfactant concentration and reaction temperature. Solution-based synthesis can produce highly crystalline nanocrystals with diverse shapes and offers notable advantages over conventional top-down methods. We synthesize various types of nanocrystals, including core/shell QDs, nanorods, nanotetrapods, and nanoporous materials (Fig. 4a). We have also reported supra-QDs (SQDs) (Fig. 4b), which are hierarchical superstructures composed of hundreds of individual QDs, each only a few nanometers in size, assembled through oriented attachment. These SQDs may exhibit enhanced charge-carrier mobility and therefore show strong potential as sensitizers for solar-cell applications.
2. Investigation of the properties of NPs induced by the incorporation of foreign atoms
Introducing foreign atoms into as-synthesized nanocrystals can alter their optical, electrical, and magnetic properties in addition to changing their composition. Depending on the amount and distribution of the introduced species, this process can be classified in several ways. One representative approach is doping, in which semiconductor nanocrystals are modified in a manner analogous to the doping of bulk semiconductors.
Doping is the intentional incorporation of foreign atoms into a pristine semiconductor host material to modulate its optical, electrical, and magnetic properties. In bulk semiconductors, dopants ionize and provide additional electrons or holes depending on their valence states. In the case of transition-metal dopants, the dopant spin can couple with the orbitals of the host material. Because of these characteristics, doped semiconductors are widely used in semiconductor junction structures, including transistors and diodes.
In semiconductor nanocrystals, however, doping is strongly affected by quantum confinement and therefore produces behaviors distinct from those observed in bulk materials. The confinement of excitons within an extremely small volume enhances their interaction with dopant ions, amplifying changes in optoelectronic and magnetic properties. Doped nanocrystals therefore have potential applications in memory devices, photocatalysts, and bioimaging probes, in addition to conventional semiconductor junction structures.
Cation exchange is another method for introducing foreign atoms into a crystal lattice. Because bonding in many semiconductor nanocrystals has substantial ionic character, newly introduced cations can replace original cations while preserving the anion framework. This transformation enables the synthesis of sophisticated nanostructures, including metastable crystal phases and complex morphologies that are difficult to access through direct synthesis.
By controlling the amount of foreign ions, cation exchange can be used for doping, heterostructure formation, or the synthesis of entirely new materials. The exchange reaction is driven by differences in the thermodynamic stability of the reactants and products, as well as by ligand-mediated complexation under specific reaction conditions. The feasibility of a given exchange reaction can be evaluated by considering the reaction conditions, solubility products, and standard enthalpies of formation of the relevant materials (Fig 5).
In nanocrystals, even when the constituent materials are identical, the crystal structures obtained after cation exchange can differ depending on particle size because thermodynamic stability is size-dependent (Fig. 6). Therefore, investigating how cation-exchange outcomes vary with nanocrystal size is important for understanding the reaction mechanism. After cation exchange, optical spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and other atomic-level characterization methods should be used to confirm the composition and crystal structure of the final material.
3. PL modulation of QD
The emission wavelength and intensity of QDs can be modulated, making them promising materials for switchable probes in cellular and whole-body imaging, optical modulation, and light-emitting devices. We used quasi type-II QDs to develop photoluminescence-modulating probes that respond to external stimuli. Charging quasi type-II QDs, in which electrons and holes are spatially separated, induces photoluminescence (PL) spectral switching. The initial emission state can be recovered through a subsequent neutralization step. Reversible PL switching over many repeated cycles was demonstrated by alternating UV excitation between on and off states (Fig. 7). We also developed a modulation sensor based on a PL on/off system. In addition, reversible and wavelength-selective PL modulation was investigated by controlling charge transfer between QDs and quenchers.
4. QD-based Solar Cells
A solar cell (SC) converts light energy directly into electrical energy. Although silicon SCs have been commercialized on a large scale, they remain costly and require complex fabrication processes. Nanocrystal-based SCs offer a potentially simpler and more cost-effective alternative. Several types of SCs use QDs, including QD-sensitized SCs, hybrid SCs composed of QDs and conducting polymers (Fig. 8), and Schottky-type SCs.
Although these SCs have different device architectures, they all rely on light absorption followed by charge generation, separation, and transport. Charge separation and transfer are influenced by the morphology of the QDs and the structure of the active layer. The use of QDs allows the absorption wavelength to be tuned, and their colloidal dispersibility in various solvents enables solution-processable device fabrication. Therefore, QD-based SCs represent a promising research direction for developing low-cost solar-energy conversion technologies. By identifying the conditions required for high power conversion efficiency, experimental studies can provide insights into simple and scalable fabrication strategies for QD-based SCs.

tabs.label: Nanoplasmonics
tabs.text:
Nanoplasmonics
Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) arises when free electrons in metal nanoparticles collectively oscillate in resonance with incident electromagnetic energy at the interface between the metal and the surrounding dielectric medium. Noble metal nanoparticles exhibit strong SPR when their dimensions are reduced to the nanoscale, and their optical properties can be precisely tuned by controlling the metal composition, particle size and shape, and local dielectric environment. These tunable SPR characteristics make noble metal nanoparticles highly versatile platforms for spectroscopic analysis, optical imaging, sensing, and therapeutic applications. Our group develops advanced metal nanoparticle complexes for highly efficient cancer therapy and photoacoustic-guided drug delivery.
Properties of Surface Plasmon Resonance
Conductive metals contain a high density of free electrons that are not strongly localized to individual atoms. Because these electrons can collectively respond to external electromagnetic fields, metallic nanostructures can exhibit surface plasmon resonance (SPR) when their dimensions are reduced to the nanoscale. SPR gives metal nanoparticles unique optical properties. In particular, noble metal nanoparticles, such as gold and silver nanoparticles, interact strongly with visible light and exhibit intense absorption and scattering, with optical cross sections that are orders of magnitude larger than those of typical organic dyes. They also show high resistance to oxidation and photobleaching, making them powerful optical probes that can complement or replace conventional organic fluorophores.
The optical responses of noble metal nanoparticles are highly tunable because their plasmon resonance can be controlled by the dielectric properties of the metal, as well as by the size, shape, and local environment of the nanostructure. Our goal is to design and synthesize diverse metallic nanostructures and to investigate their optical properties using spectroscopic and imaging tools. We further aim to apply these nanostructures to biological and biomedical systems (Fig. 1).
Study of Thermotherapy for Tumor Cells
Photothermal therapy is a cancer treatment strategy in which absorbed photon energy is converted into heat to induce cancer cell death (Fig. 2). Because cancer cells are generally more sensitive to elevated temperatures than normal cells, selective heat generation within tumor tissues can improve therapeutic efficacy while reducing damage to surrounding healthy tissue. Metal nanoparticles are highly effective photothermal agents because of their strong light absorption and efficient photothermal conversion. By controlling the thermal energy generated through the photothermal effect of metal nanoparticles, selective cancer therapy can be achieved.
Near-infrared (NIR) light is widely used for photothermal therapy because it penetrates deeply into living tissues and is only weakly absorbed or scattered by major biomolecules such as hemoglobin and water. The therapeutic selectivity of pH-responsive “smart” gold nanoparticles that absorb NIR light preferentially in cancer cells or tumor tissues can be further enhanced by exploiting the acidic and hypoxic microenvironment of tumors. In addition, nanoparticle-mediated photothermal treatment can be combined with anticancer drugs to achieve synergistic therapeutic effects. Gold nanoparticle aggregation can be induced through various strategies. For example, DNA hydrogel–nanoparticle complexes can be designed to release anticancer drugs while simultaneously promoting nanoparticle aggregation, providing a platform for combined photothermal and chemotherapeutic treatment (Fig 3).
Dark-Field Microscopy
Dark-field microscopy (DFM) visualizes scattered light from a specimen, whereas conventional transmission-mode microscopy forms images using transmitted light. Metal nanoparticles can generate strong contrast under DFM because they efficiently scatter incident light at wavelengths that match their SPR. Because scattering signals from small metal nanoparticles are intense and highly sensitive to plasmonic properties, DFM enables optical visualization even at the single-particle level.
DFM is also useful for distinguishing materials that may show only weak contrast in conventional imaging modes. This capability allows the SPR properties of individual metal nanoparticles to be characterized and enables biological imaging using metal nanoparticles as scattering-based contrast agents (Fig. 4).
Photoacoustic Imaging Using “Smart” Gold Nanoparticles
Photoacoustic imaging (PAI) is an emerging hybrid imaging modality that combines optical excitation with ultrasound detection. As a nonionizing biomedical imaging method, PAI can provide molecular and functional information, including hemoglobin oxygen saturation, blood flow, and tissue morphology. It is therefore well suited for biomedical studies, including the monitoring of tumor physiology and treatment responses.
In PAI, image contrast is determined by the optical absorption properties of the target. Exogenous contrast agents with strong near-infrared (NIR) absorption can enhance PA signals because NIR light penetrates deeply into biological tissues. “Smart” gold nanoparticles (SANs) can rapidly aggregate under mildly acidic conditions, which are commonly found in tumor microenvironments. This aggregation induces a red shift in their absorption spectrum toward the red and NIR regions. As a result, PA amplitude increases under mildly acidic conditions while remaining relatively unchanged at physiological pH. By combining tumor accumulation with high PA conversion efficiency, SANs can significantly amplify PA signals in cell-level and small-animal experiments (Fig. 6). These properties make SANs a promising platform for PA-guided drug delivery, enabling real-time identification of delivery targets and on-demand therapeutic administration.

tabs.label: Nanobiotechnology
tabs.text:
Nanobiotechnology
QD-based optical probes provide a promising platform for in vivo bioimaging and next-generation medical imaging applications because of their bright luminescence, resistance to photobleaching, and size-tunable emission wavelengths. Our group develops NIR-II-emitting QD probes and has demonstrated cancer diagnosis using QD–antibody conjugates. We have also engineered amphiphilic polyethylenimine-derivative platforms that incorporate QDs for cell labeling, targeted delivery, gene delivery, and ratiometric oxygen sensing.
1. Biological applications of Quantum dots
Semiconductor QDs present a possible new technology for in vivo bio-imaging and future medical-imaging applications. QDs have proven potential as imaging contrast agents due to their bright luminescence, their resistance to photobleaching, and their tunable emission wavelengths. The main impediment to the use of QDs for biological applications is their biocompatibility. QDs that contain toxic elements such as Cd, Pb, Hg, or As have limited biological applications. High quality ‘non-toxic’ QDs have been synthesized (e.g., InP, ZnTe/ZnSe, CuInS2; AgInS2); they are free from potential leakage of toxic heavy-metal ions, and photoluminesce at wavelengths that can be selected by adjusting the size of the QD. The new methods of synthesizing ‘non-toxic’ QDs using various solvents and QD precursors have been investigated to obtain bright and photostable QDs that promise application to in vivo medical imaging.
2. Surface modification, functionalization and bioconjugation of QDs for biological applications
QDs are synthesized in inorganic solvent to obtain high quality, so their surfaces should be modified for bioimaging applications. The surface molecules for QDs should give good colloidal stabilities in aqueous solutions without aggregation, and should have appropriate sites to allow conjugation with biomolecules. To be suitable for applications in targeted imaging or in long-term in vivo imaging, QDs must be colloidally stable and must have minimal non-specific binding. QDs that have been modified to have zwitterionic surface molecules can maintain colloidal stability over broad ranges of pH and ionic strength, and to show minimal non-specific adsorptions (Fig. 1). Moreover, the zwitterionic QD surface ligands can also be used in conjunction with other functional groups; this trait allows simple conjugations for highly specific targeting while retaining the advantages of a zwitterionic QD surface (Fig. 2).
3. Cancer Diagnosis Using QD - Antibody Conjugates
Cancer is a very heterogeneous system. Multiplexed QD imaging is well-suited to detecting such heterogeneous systems. QDs are also bright, photostable, and allow multiplexing by a single excitation wavelength. QDs have broad absorption profile with large one-photon and two-photon absorption cross sections, narrow and symmetric emission profile, and large effective Stokes shifts. To improve the accuracy of cancer detection, multiple biological targets must be imaged concurrently; these advantages of QDs can be used in multiplexing to achieve fluorescence molecular imaging of cancer tissues. Doctors frequently use endoscopy to detect colon cancer, but the diagnosis is based on the clinician's naked-eye perception, which is subjective and error-prone.We developed a rapid and accurate molecular fluorescence imaging technique that uses antibody (Ab)-coated QDs (Ab-QDs) that are sprayed and washed simultaneously on colon tumor tissues inside live animals, then excited and imaged by endoscopy. QDs were conjugated to matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) 9, MMP 14, or carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) Abs with zwitterionic surface coating to reduce nonspecific bindings. The Ab-QD probes can diagnose tumors on sectioned mouse tissues, in fresh mouse colons stained ex vivo and in vivo, and in fresh human colon adenoma tissues in 30 min and can be imaged to a depth of 100 μm. The probes successfully detected not only cancers that are readily discernible to the naked eye, but also hyperplasia and adenoma regions. Sum and cross-signal operations provided post-processed images that can show complementary information or regions of high priority (Fig. 3). This multiplexed QD, spray-and-wash, and endoscopy approach provides a significant advantage for detecting small or flat tumors that may be missed by conventional endoscopic examinations and bestows a strategy for the improvement of cancer diagnosis.
4. NIR-II emitting QD probes
The NIR biological window from 650 nm to 1700 nm allows deeper penetration than visible light into biological tissues such as skin and blood, because these tissues scatter and absorb less light at long wavelengths than at short wavelengths. The window between 650 nm and 950 nm (NIR-I) has been exploited extensively for in vivo optical imaging of live animals, but little research has considered use of the longer-wavelength window (NIR-II) from 1000 to 1700 nm for in vivo fluorescence imaging of live animals. Light scattering and absorption by biomolecules are much weaker in the NIR-II region than in NIR-I, so tissue penetration depth and spatial resolution are increased, and autofluorescence is decreased in NIR-II. QDs can be advantageous fluorescent probes for molecular imaging in both the NIR-I and the NIR-II region. CdTeSe, and CuInS2 have been developed as fluorophores in NIR-I, and have shown high photostability and quantum yield (QY) > 50%. PbS and Ag2S QDs have been developed for NIR-II fluorescence imaging applications, and showed QY > 10% with inorganic shells in the aqueous phase (Fig. 4). We report an enzyme-activatable NIR-II probe that exhibits fluorescence (FL) upon matrix metalloprotease activity in tumor microenvironment. Bright and stable PbS/CdS/ZnS core/shell/shell QDs were synthesized as a model NIR-II fluorophore, and activatable modulators were attached to exploit photoexcited electron transfer (PET) quenching. The quasi-type-II QD band alignment allowed rapid and effective FL modulations with a compact surface ligand modulator that contains methylene blue PET quencher. The modulator was optimized to afford full enzyme accessibility and high activation signal surge when the enzyme was active. In a colon-cancer mouse model, the probe demonstrated selective FL activation at tumor sites with tripled signal strength in 10 min (Fig. 5).
We report an enzyme-activatable NIR-II probe that exhibits fluorescence (FL) upon matrix metalloprotease activity in tumor microenvironment. Bright and stable PbS/CdS/ZnS core/shell/shell QDs were synthesized as a model NIR-II fluorophore, and activatable modulators were attached to exploit photoexcited electron transfer (PET) quenching. The quasi type-II QD band alignment allowed rapid and effective FL modulations with a compact surface ligand modulator that contains methylene blue PET quencher. The modulator was optimized to afford full enzyme accessibility and high activation signal surge when the enzyme was active. Using a colon cancer mouse model, the probe demonstrated selective FL activation at tumor sites with tripled signal strength in 10 min (Fig. 5).
5. Sensing molecule by using QDs
Amphiphilic polyethyleneimine derivatives (amPEIs) were synthesized and used to encapsulate dozens of QDs. The QD-amPEI composite was ~100 nm in hydrodynamic diameter and had an outer surface with a slight positive charge that is well suited for cellular internalization. The outer positive surface was further exploited for gene delivery and targeting. Co-delivery of QDs and GFP-silencing RNAs was demonstrated by attaching siRNAs to the outer surface; the process achieved transfection efficiency that was an order of magnitude higher than conventional gene transfections. Hyaluronic acids were tethered onto the QD-amPEI for cell-specific targeted labeling, which achieved a specific-to-nonspecific signal ratio > 100. The inside hydrophobic compartment was further applied to cohost oxygen-sensing phosphorescence Ru dyes along with QDs. The ratiometric PL signals of the QD-Ru-amPEI oxygen probe show accurate and reversible oxygen-sensing capability and were successfully applied to cellular and spheroid models (Fig. 6).

Chemical-Based Aging Research Lab
Chang Lab aims to develop live senescent cell probes and control the aging process, by chemical or photodynamic approach.
overview:
DOFL compounds are generated by combinatorial modification of organic fluorescent scaffolds, where simple building blocks can be assembled with the aim of creating diverse compounds. The design and preparation of DOFL focus on exploring the diverse chemical space directly around a fluorescent scaffold. This approach provides some advantages in the development of bioimaging probes since it can be applied without knowledge about the target molecule and an additional reporter is not required for the visualization of the probes. Therefore, DOFLA depends entirely on the structural diversity of the fluorescence library empowered by the unbiased evaluation of compounds to identify target-selective fluorescent probes. DOFL derived from fluorescence scaffolds such as rosamine, BODIPY, chalcone, and xanthone covers a very wide range of chemical space and fluorescence spectra (400−800 nm).
We have developed more than 30 livel cell probes and figured out the unique mechanisms. HOLD (Holding-Oriented Live-cell Distinction) probes have binding biomarkers on or inside the target cells. The biomarkers can be proteins, carbohydrates, DNA, etc. GOLD (Gating-Oriented Live-cell Distinction) probes selectively enter or are excluded from target cells through specific transporters. GOLD probes are substrates of transporters, whose cell-type-specific accumulation is majorly dependent on transporters. LOLD (Lipid-Oriented Live-cell Distinction) probes are loaded on the target cell membrane through a kinetically controlled membrane fusion. MOLD (Metabolism-Oriented Live-cell Distinction) probes selectively stain target cells through a unique metabolism.

Primary areas of interest
Brief introduction to our research field
(NAS-KAST symposium)
In our ongoing research, we are dedicated to advancing the realms of photochemical and electrochemical organic synthesis. Our primary goal is to redefine photo- and electrocatalysis, enabling the efficient synthesis of value-added molecules from raw chemical feedstock.
We endeavor to pioneer a fresh conceptual framework, pushing the boundaries of both photochemical and electrochemical synthetic organic methodologies. Through our exploration of innovative approaches, we strive to contribute to the creation of sustainable and economically feasible pathways in organic synthesis, utilizing state-of-the-art photochemical and electrocatalytic techniques.
Furthermore, we are concurrently conducting research that applies insights gleaned from the electrochemical behavior of organic and organometallic molecules observed in these processes to the development of organic-based battery materials such as organic electrolytes and solvents.

overview:
Lecture
Polymer actuators
Electroactive ionic polymer actuators
Electroactive actuators that show reversible mechanical deformation in response to an electric field have received enormous interest in the era of biomimetic technology such as artificial muscles, robotics and microsensors. Recently, ionic polymer actuators comprising a layer of polymer electrolyte sandwiched in between electrodes have emerged as promising candidates in such applications, owing to their lightweight, flexibility, mechanical robustness and ease of fabrication at low cost. The most important requirements are large displacements in bending motion, fast response time, low operating voltage and durability in air.
We developed new ionic polymer actuators comprising phase-separated block copolymers and ionic liquids. [Figure 1] The use of sulfonated block copolymer possessing well-connected ionic channels resulted in fast response and the best performance under sub-1V condition, in comparison to the state-of-the-art PVdF-based actuators, upon building up efficient ion conduction pathway. In-situ SAXS experiments were carried out to underpin the actuation mechanism of the new actuator and the key to success stemmed from the evolution of the unique nanostructure of the electrolyte layer with dimensional gradients beneath the cathode during actuation, which promoted the bending motion of the actuators. (Kim, O. et al. Nature Communications 2013, 4, 2208.)
Figure 1. Electroactive actuators based on nanostructured copolymers and comparison of actuation mechanism between block copolymer/PVdF(HFP)
Furthermore, we investigated the electromechanical properties of ionic polymer actuators to unveil key factors affecting the actuation performance. [Figure 2] First, the extent of electromechanical deformation of the actuators was proven to be largely affected by the type of anion in the ILs, as understood by the anion-dependent ionic conductivity, charging time, and Young’s modulus of IL-containing polymers. Second, we show that the bending strain and durability of the actuators are tunable in a straightforward manner by controlling the block architecture and molecular weight of the polymer, where the use of triblock copolymers was found to be beneficial in enhancing the actuation performance. Lastly, our actuators demonstrated up to a 10 times increase in the bending strain, compared to actuators based on conventional PVdF-HFP with the same type of IL. The key to success stemmed from the self-assembled structure of sulfonated block copolymers having continuous ionic phases with highly interactive −SO3H surfaces, which facilitated fast ion diffusion with a reduced tendency to form ion clusters. (Kim, O. et al. Macromolecules, 2014, 47 (13), 4357.)
Figure 2. Actuation performances depending on voltage/frequency/IL types/polymers
Our results convince that the nanostructured block copolymer electrolytes allow the successful actuator operation with a small battery, which paves the way for advanced biomimetic technologies in the future. [Figure 3] Furthermore, the actuation performance may be tuned by varying the type of ionic liquids and by employing a range of block copolymers with different molecular weights and compositions. In addition, experiments on whether the morphology effects and development of new types of actuators for practical biomimetic devices are present in the actuators will be subjects of future studies.
Figure 3. Actuators in artificial fingers

areas.name: Lithium battery
areas.text:
Lithium battery
Lithium battery
Lithium battery
Recently, Li-ion batteries (LIBs) have drawn significant attention due to the various applications to power portable electronics and electric vehicles (EV) since they have highest energy densities among commercialized secondary batteries. However, it is highly demanded to develop the next generation LIBs in terms of power density, rate capability, and electrochemical stability. In order to improve these performances, nanostructured energy materials as electrolyte and electrode of LIBs have been extensively studies.
Until now, polymer electrolytes are replacing carbonate based conventional liquid electrolyte owing to advanced safety and cycle life. However, they are insufficient to prevent lithium dendrite growth which induced cell short circuit. The realization of high mechanical strength from polymer electrolytes promote a wide variety of strategies to synthesize new polymer electrolytes comprising PEO chains and mechanically robust counterparts have been proposed. Herein, block copolymer electrolyte and composite polymer electrolyte have been studied as candidate materials possessing high mechanical strength and ionic conductivity simultaneously.
(1) Block copolymer electrolyte
Among solid electrolytes, block copolymer electrolyte in which hard polymers and PEO are covalently attached are attractive material having synergistic combination of phase separation behavior and ion transport property. The poly(styrene-b-ethylene oxide) (PS-b-PEO) block copolymer is one of representative block copolymer exhibiting strongly segregated PS and PEO phases in the nanometer scale, which allows the structural integrity to be maintained by effectively confining the lithium salt within the PEO domains. While such research efforts have opened new prospects in the era of high-conductivity solid-state electrolytes, defined as having a conductivity of ~10−5 S·cm−1 at room temperature. In addition, coexisting non-conducting hard polymers influence lithium-ion diffusion across PEO domains due to interfacial mixing, which leads to lower lithium transport rates than predicted.
This has motivated researchers to study the relationship between the nanostructure and conductivity of lithium salt-doped PS-b-PEO block copolymers and a variety of observations concerning the morphology effects have been reported. However, the difficulties in correlating morphological effects on conductivity arises from the fact that the different molecular weights and compositions of block copolymers themselves also influence ion diffusion coefficients, which are tied to ion transport properties. Herein a method for the precise control over nanoscale morphology of polymer electrolytes was reported by introducing functional terminal group substitution.
A set of poly(styrene-b-ethylene oxide) (PS-b-PEO) block copolymers having dissimilar PEO end groups (−OH, −SO3H, −SO3Li, and −COOH) were successfully synthesized by means of anionic polymerization technique. These polymers were doped by bis(trifluoromethane) sulfonamide lithium salt (LiTFSI) with specific ratios. Neat and salt doped block copolymers exhibited various self-assembled morphologies including disordered, lamellar, gyroid, and hexagonal cylindrical phases.
Decreased conductivity was observed for PS-b-PEO tethered with acid groups when doped with lithium salts, which we ascribe to the slow segmental motion of acid group-terminated PEO chains. However, normalized conductivity of acid tethered samples are identical, or even exceeding hydroxyl terminated sample. Furthermore. organization of the PEO domains of PS-b-PEO with terminal acid units into self-assembled nanostructures having sharp interfaces proved beneficial for increasing ion transport efficiency by creating less tortuous ion conduction pathways. Our results suggest a unique methodology for controlling the morphology and ion transport properties of block copolymer electrolytes via attachment of a single end functional unit.
Figure 1. (a) Transmission electron micrographs (b) Normalized conductivity (σnor)
(Jo, G. et al. Polymer Journal 2016)
(2) Composite polymer electrolyte
Gel polymer electrolytes (GPEs) characterized by conducting matrix and cross-linked polymeric network generally have higher ionic conductivities than solid polymer electrolyte. However, GPEs still have low mechanical strength unable to block the dendrite growth. From this standpoint, the fabrication of composite gel polymer electrolytes (CPEs) by incorporating nanosized inorganic fillers into the GPEs is being explored.
Free-standing CPEs with ca. 80 mm thickness were prepared by mixing silica nanoparticles (SNPs), polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA), and lithium salt-doped tetraethylene glycol dimethyl ether (TEGDME), followed by UV curing for 3 min at room temperature. These CPEs impart improved mechanical properties without significant loss of ionic conductivity. During synthesized, it was found that while a simple UV curing procedure results in the homogeneous distribution of SNPs in cross-linked PEO matrices (referred to as hCPE), a thermal pre-treatment at 80 ℃ causes the CPE to maintain SNP density gradients in the thickness direction of the CPE (denser at air surfaces, attributed to low surface tension of the SNPs).
Synthesized CPEs were applied as lithium sulfur battery electrolyte offering the suppression of shuttling of lithium polysulfide intermediates between the electrodes, owing to the presence of physical barriers (high negative charge of −47 mV) when the polysulfides reach the liquid electrolytes. The lithium salt dissociation also promoted by incorporating high dielectric constant inorganic materials with a large surface area.
The exploitation of CPE enabled us to attain a stable discharge capacity of 970 mA·h·g−1 after 100 cycles. The improved long-term cycle life is believed to be as a result of the strategic positioning of negatively charged SNPs near the cathode surfaces, in order to decelerate the dissolution of polysulfides into the CPE during battery cycling. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to unveil the important role played by the internal structure of the CPEs in determining the performance of Li–S cells.
Figure 2. (a) Schematic illustration of the fabrication procedure for hCPE and gCPE (b) ) representative voltage profiles of the Li/gCPE/S-C cell (c) Discharge/charge capacities of the Li/gCPE/S-GDL cell obtained with cycling.
(Choi, I. et al. RSC Adv. 2014 , 4 , 61333 )
(3) Cathode material
Elemental sulfur is one of the most attractive cathode active materials in lithium batteries because of its high theoretical specific capacity. Despite the positive aspect, lithium–sulfur batteries have suffered from severe capacity fading and limited rate capability. In this study, we develop advanced Li-S batteries by synthesizing a series of organic crystals based on trithiocyanuric acid having two functional groups of thiol and amine. Two crystal structures were obtained from different crystallization solvents; a unique square tube with hierarchical pores, i.e., micron-scale hole in the tube and abundant micropores at the surfaces, and a splice plate with only micropores at the surfaces. Our study demonstrated that the tubular crystals with hierarchical pores serve as a model system for confining sulfur and accommodating the volumetric expansion during cycling, as shown by long-life and excellent capacity retention. Under optimized conditions, our Li-S cell can deliver reversible discharge capacity of 1100 mAh/g at 0.2C with stable cycling performance over 300 cycles, corresponding to capacity retention of 90% from the initial discharge capacity. In addition to the good capacity retention property of our Li-S cell, improved rate performance was also determined. The Li-S cell based on the tubular organic crystal/sulfur composite cathode was found to deliver a reversible capacity of 900 mAh/g at 2C. After cycling at various rates, further cycling at a low rate of 0.2C brings it back to a reversible capacity of 1100 mAh/g. The markedly improved cycling performance of our Li-S cell is attributed to the increased Li+-ion transport of the organic crystal/sulfur composite cathode along amine moieties of crystal frameworks, as determined by Randles-Sevcik analysis.
Figure 3. Synthetic route of sulfur-rich polymers
(Kim, H. et al. Nat. Commun. 2015 , 6, 7278)

areas.name: Chemical sensor
areas.text:
Chemical sensor
Chemical sensor
Chemical sensors based on polymeric materials have been widely investigated since it is easy to amplify the signal and fabricate into practical forms such like solutions, films, and free-standing membranes. These concepts need characteristic interaction between polymers and target molecules such as heavy metal ions, warfare agents, and bio-materials giving a measurable signal in response like fluorescence, color, and structure changes. Among the different types of sensor, Fluorescent polymer sensors have received great deal of attention due to their ability to detect targets at low concentrations and easily measurable optical event. To improve the sensing ability, various functional groups have been introduced into sensor applications and moreover, Self-assembled polymer electrolytes which used can form the specific structures have been used it can lead to the spatial benefits for effective interactions or dynamic changes in structure and signal response.
In this regard, our group reported the new ratiometric pH sensor based on poly(N-phenylmaleimide) (PPMI)-containing block copolymer that emits three different fluorescent colors depending on the pH. The strong solvatochromism and tautomerism of the PPMI derivatives enabled precise pH sensing for almost the entire range of the pH scale. Theoretical calculations have predicted largely dissimilar band gaps for the keto, enol, and enolate tautomers of PPMI owing to lowdimensional conjugation effects. The tunable emission wavelength and intensity of our sensors, as well as the reversible color switching with high-luminescent contrast, were achieved using rational molecular design of PPMI analogues as an innovative platform for accurate H+ detection. The self-assembly of block copolymers on the nanometer length scale was particularly highlighted as a novel prospective means of regulating fluorescence properties while avoiding the self-quenching phenomenon, and this system can be used as a fast responsive pH sensor in versatile device forms.
Figure 1. (a) TEM micrographs of the micelles of 0.2 wt % 2a in aqueous media at different pH conditions. Schematic illustrations depicting pH-sensitive micellar morphologies are given in the inset graphics of (a). (b) Fluorescence micrographs of thin film
(Ahn, H. et al. ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces 2015 , 7 , 704-712)
We developed the effective fluorescence sensor using sulfonated block copolymer electrolytes to detect Cu(II) ions in aqueous media. Due to the several benefits from self-assembly and functional groups, this sensor can be considered as a powerful sensor. Research on the development of self-assembled fluorescence sensors is also being performed continuously in our lab and we expect that fluorescence polymer sensors become a promising materials for sensory system to apply into pollutant sensors, medical diagnosis, and real-life applications.
Figure 2. Self-assembled polymer electrolytes and its sensing ability toward Cu(II) ions.
(Ahn, H. et al. ACS Nano 2013 , 7 , 6162-6169)
As the other type of chemical sensors, polymeric humidity sensors which exhibit the change of their physical property depending on humidity have been extensively investigated in past decades. To our knowledge, polymeric humidity sensors usually need a few minutes to change their physical property in response to humidity change. In contrast, a humidity sensor developed by our lab, exhibit extremely fast self-displayed discernible reflective color changes from violet to red, and a few orders of magnitude changes in impedance with exposure to humid air, at the same time. It is due to the fact that nanostructures can help water diffusion through short pathways in nanometer scales and it can be the powerful tools for food industry, medical science, and electronic applications.
Figure 3. Humidity sensors and its performance
(Kim, E. et al. ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2012 , 4 , 5179-5187)

areas.name: PEMFC
areas.text:
PEMFC
PEMFC
PEM
Proton exchange fuel cell (PEFC) has been extensively investigated in past decades due to their potential to supply clean energy for transport applications.
Figure 1. Schematic illustration of fuel cell vehicle and fuel cell stack
In early years, the researches on PEFC had focused on room temperature operation, and many issues such as CO poisoning of Pt catalyst and the complexity of water management in polymer electrolyte membranes (PEMs) have been revealed. Several approaches are in progress to overcome these problems, and operating PEFC at high temperature above 120 °C under nonhumidification conditions is considered to be the most promising solution. For the high temperature PEFC, there is a growing need to find new PEM systems offering reasonable proton conductivity without water.
In our lab, we developed new PEM systems, which is the fabrication of composite PEMs by incorporating ionic liquids (ILs) to replace water molecule in the block copolymer matrices. Compared with membranes having discrete ionic domains (including Nafion 117), our membranes revealed over an order of magnitude increase in conductivity with the highest conductivity of 0.045 S/cm obtained at 165 °C by inducing the nanostructure. We investigate the relationship between the morphology and the conductivity of PEMs comprising diverse ILs highlighting the important role of the types of self-assembled structures in determining the transport efficiency.
Figure 2. The relationship between morphology and conductivity in PEM electrolytes
(Kim, S. Y. et. al. Nat. Commun. 2010, 1, 88, Kim, S. Y. et. al. Macromolecules, 2011, 44 (13), 5289, Kim, O. et. al. Macromolecules, 2012, 45 (21), 8702.)
In addition, we explore the fascinating experimental insights into confinement- and interface-driven modulation of ion transport properties for polymer electrolytes and study valuable insights into the factors affecting the proton transport efficiency of IL-containing polymers. Our research would provide the future prospects for designing desired nanostructures as efficient PEFCs.
Figure 3. The factors affecting the ion transport properties (a) The effect of dissimilar internal structures on conductivity (b) Proton transference number of PEM containing various ILs. (Kim, O. et. al. J. Phys. Chem. Lett., 2013, 4 (13), 2111, Kim, S. Y. et. al. Macromolecules, 2014, 47(3), 1099.)
Nowadays, we developed a new block copolymers tailored with phosphonic acid as a protogenic group. The direct comparison with sulfonated block copolymers was allowed to elucidate the role of the protogenic group in determining the phase behavior of acid-containing polymers. We first reported nanostructured phosphonated polymers which have the potential to be alternatives to the widely studied sulfonated polymers. Our research would provide the future prospects for designing desired nanostructures as efficient PEFCs.
Figure 4. The various nanostructures of phosphonated block copolymers containing ILs
(Jung, H. Y. et. al. Macomolecules, 2015, 48(17), 6142, Jung, H. Y. et. al. Macromol. Rapid Commun., 2016)

overview:
Our Vision and Philosophy
Climate change is one of the most pressing environmental challenges facing humanity.
The ultimate goal of our research group is to improve our ability to predict the future evolution of the climate system driven by anthropogenic forcing and natural variability.
We believe that understanding the physics of the climate system is essential for making reliable predictions of future climate. Accordingly, we develop and apply quantitative approaches to studying the climate system and elucidating the physical mechanisms governing its variability and change.
We pursue fundamental advances in climate science across a broad range of directions, including the development of new conceptual frameworks, theories, and models, the discovery of previously unrecognized phenomena, and the resolution of long-standing problems in the field. Through these efforts, we aim to open new research directions and push the frontiers of climate science.
Our Focus
Our research is rooted in large-scale climate dynamics, with an emphasis on coupled atmosphere–ocean processes and their broader interactions with the cryosphere and terrestrial systems. Spatially, our research spans from the tropics to the polar regions. Temporally, we focus on present-day and future climate, while occasionally drawing on paleoclimate records to better understand the long-term evolution and sensitivity of the climate system.
We use an integrated approach that combines observations, theory, and a hierarchy of models spanning a broad range of complexity—from simple conceptual models to fully coupled Earth system models—alongside emerging AI-based approaches.
Research Themes
Our research centers on two interconnected themes.
1. Future Climate Change Dynamics
A central challenge in climate science is to understand and predict how the climate system will respond to anthropogenic warming. While many aspects of climate change evolve gradually, some of the most consequential changes may arise from abrupt, nonlinear, or unexpected responses of the climate system. We investigate these high-impact responses across major components of the climate system and seek to uncover the physical mechanisms, critical thresholds, and interactions that shape future climate trajectories.
Abrupt Climate Change
Investigating critical thresholds, nonlinear processes, and cascading interactions associated with abrupt changes in major climate elements, including ocean circulation, monsoon systems, ice sheets, and terrestrial ecosystems.
Emergent Climate Phenomena
Identifying new climate behaviors that may emerge—or existing phenomena that may disappear—as the climate system warms, including novel extremes, variability modes, circulation patterns, and precipitation regimes.
Irreversibility and Climate Recovery
Assessing the reversibility and recovery potential of the climate system under mitigation scenarios, including emission reductions, net-zero pathways, and carbon dioxide removal.
2. Climate Variability Modes and Global Impacts
The climate system exhibits large-scale modes of natural variability that drive fluctuations from interannual to decadal timescales and influence weather and environmental systems worldwide. We study major modes of climate variability, including the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the Indian Ocean Dipole, and modes of variability in the polar regions. We seek to understand their underlying dynamics, improve their predictability, and quantify their influence on the global climate and environmental systems.
Dynamics and Predictability
Developing physics-based theories and modeling frameworks to explain the fundamental dynamics of major climate variability modes and improve predictions of their intensity, frequency, and evolution.
Interactions with Global Warming
Investigating the two-way interactions through which anthropogenic warming alters climate variability, while climate variability modulates the timing, rate, and regional patterns of warming.
Impacts on Global Environmental Systems
Quantifying how climate variability affects hydrological extremes, heatwaves, wildfires, marine heatwaves, coral bleaching, and regional precipitation through atmospheric and oceanic teleconnections.

Climate Change Research Lab
We are advancing our understanding of global and regional climate change and its impacts.
overview:
Climate Change Detection and Attribution (기후변화 탐지 및 원인규명)
Understanding the causes of the observed climate change is fundamental to the reliable future projections of climate changes. In particular, quantifying human contribution to the observed climate changes at regional and local scales is challenging due mainly to the stronger influence of natural climate variability. Climate change ‘detection’ is defined as the process of demonstrating that an observed change is significantly different from natural internal variability, and ‘attribution’ means the process of isolation of the causes of the detected change. In order to identify human influences on climate in separation from natural factors, we compare the space-time patterns of observed changes with those from climate model simulations integrated under different forcings (such as man-made increases in greenhouse gases and sulfate aerosols, and natural changes in solar and volcanic activities) using a sophisticated statistical technique so-called ‘optical fingerprinting’.
[“Human-caused Indo-Pacific warm pool expansion” (Weller et al. 2016, Science Advances)]
[“Human contribution to more-intense precipitation extremes” (Min et al. 2011, Nature)]

areas.name: Climate Extremes
areas.text:
Climate extremes and natural climate variability (극한기후와 자연변동성)
Stronger impacts of climate changes occur with changes in the frequency and intensity of extreme weather and climate events such as heat waves, cold snaps, droughts, and heavy precipitation. However, climate extremes occur at smaller-spatial and shorter-time scales, which makes it difficult to observe and simulate them and also to identify their changes in the past and future. The small spatial scale also means the stronger influence of natural climate variability such as the El-Ninõ Southern Oscillation and the Arctic Oscillation. Therefore, one needs to better understand the influences of natural climate variability on climate extremes so as to isolate the anthropogenic influence under global warming. We conduct comprehensive analyses of the observed and model-simulated climate extremes using statistical methods based on the extreme value theory. We also employ probabilistic approaches (such as the Fraction of Attributable Risk) to quantify the human or natural contribution to the changes in the odds of climate extremes. Finally, physical mechanisms associated with the changes in extreme events are explored.
[“Influence of climate variability on extreme ocean surface wave heights assessed from ERA-Interim and ERA-20C reanalyses” (Kumar et al. 2016, J. Climate)]
[“Assessing Human contribution to the summer 2013 Korean heat wave”, Min et al. (2014, BAMS)]

areas.name: Climate Projection
areas.text:
Climate Change Projection and Mechanism (기후변화 전망 및 메커니즘)
Scientists predict future global and regional climates by simulating climate models under different forcing scenarios of greenhouse gases and aerosols emissions. Future projections of climate change are basically highly uncertain due to a few factors including scenario uncertainty, model uncertainty, and internal variability. Probabilistic future projections of climate change provide a way to take account of these uncertainties in a systematic manner. Also, evaluating relative contributions of different uncertainty sources is critical to improving our scenarios and models and thereby increasing the reliability of climate change projections. In this respect, understanding physical mechanism for future changes is critical. For instance, comparing multiple climate models in terms of thermodynamic and dynamic contributions to regional-scale precipitation changes will help to identify what is major uncertainty factor for a target region.
[“Thermodynamic and dynamic contributions to future changes in summer precipitation over Northeast Asia and Korea: A multi-RCM study”, Lee et al. (2017, Climate Dynamics)]
[“Probabilistic climate change predictions applying Bayesian model averaging”, Min et al. (2007, Phil. Trans. Roy. Soc. London)]

areas.name: Hydrological Cycle
areas.text:
Hydrological cycle and climate zone shift (수문 순환과 기후대 이동)
Hydrological cycle plays an important role in heat and energy exchanges between the atmosphere, the land, and the ocean, driving atmospheric and oceanic circulations and thereby determining global and regional climate zones. Therefore, understanding changes in the hydrological cycle under global warming is imperative to understand past and future changes in climate zone and seasonal cycle. In particular one needs to understand anthropogenic and natural mechanisms for changes in atmospheric and oceanic circulations. Recent challenging issues include the poleward expansion of Hadley cell, the impact of volcanic eruptions in the global and regional hydrological cycle, and changes in the amplitude and shape of the seasonal cycle, which are actively being studied by analyzing various observations and climate model experiments.
[“Climate responses to volcanic eruptions assessed from observations and CMIP5 multi-models” Paik and Min (2017, Climate Dyn.)]
[“Attribution of the local Hadley cell widening in the Southern Hemisphere” Kim et al. (2017, GRL)]

areas.name: Polar Climate
areas.text:
Arctic Climate and Cryosphere (북극기후와 빙권)
Arctic regions are important as an indicator of global warming, experiencing the fastest warming and sea ice loss due to ice-albedo feedback. This region is also important due to its possible impacts on the Northern Hemisphere mid-latitude climate through changes in the atmospheric circulation. Changes in Arctic precipitation can also influence global climate by inducing changes in freshwater inflow into the Arctic Ocean, which in turn affect the deep-ocean circulation. Therefore, understanding polar climate change is crucial for reliable future projections of global climate changes. More researches are needed on this issue, including the causes of the rapid Arctic sea-ice melting and its impacts on regional climates, and the space-time patterns of the recent snow cover changes and the associated physical mechanisms.
[“Human-induced Arctic moistening” Min et al. (2008, Science)]
[“Attributing Causes of 2015 Record Minimum Sea-Ice Extent in the Sea of Okhotsk” Paik et al. (2017, J. Climate)]

Hydro-Climatology Research Group
@POSTECH
Welcome to the homepage of the Hydroclimatology Research Group at POSTECH. Please follow the NEWS about our research group activities and visit other web pages: Group Members, Research Projects, Publications, Photos, Data, and Archive.
Our research interests are 1) drought mechanisms, risk, and predictability, 2) large-scale land surface modeling focusing on the land cover and use change impact, 3) river and reservoir monitoring via remote senesing and unmanned vehicles, and 4) socio-hydrology with a focus on the dynamics of social response during water-related disasters.
If you are interested in these research topics, please contact me (jhkam@postech.ac.kr)
